1.20 Wind over mountains and the altimeter

chapters.html:
Every later chapter of meteorology rests on three quantities: temperature, pressure and density. This chapter explains how they are arranged in the vertical, how the air gains and loses heat, and how the altimeter turns pressure into a height that is only correct on a standard day. Get these foundations right and wind, stability, cloud and altimetry questions become applications of the same few ideas.

1.1 Layers of the atmosphere

The atmosphere is divided into layers by how temperature changes with height, not by what the air is made of or by its pressure. In the troposphere, the lowest layer, temperature falls with height, on average by about 2 °C per 1000 ft, because the air is heated from below by the ground. The top of the troposphere is the tropopause: by the WMO definition, the lowest level at which the lapse rate falls to 2 °C per km or less and stays that small for at least 2 km above. Above it lies the stratosphere, which in the ISA is isothermal at −56.5 °C from 11 km to 20 km and then warms with height, because ozone absorbs ultraviolet sunlight. FL 650 is about 20 km, so the syllabus stops at the top of that isothermal layer. 01.01.01.01

Each layer has its own character. The troposphere holds almost all of the water vapour and is stirred by strong vertical mixing, so it is where weather happens: cloud, precipitation, icing and convection. The tropopause is a thin transition layer, broken into steps where jet streams lie. The stratosphere is very dry and very stable, since temperature constant or rising with height acts like an inversion; vertical motion is small and the wind usually weakens above the jet level. Cruise in the lower stratosphere is normally smooth and cloud-free. The exceptions are overshooting Cb tops, clear-air turbulence near the tropopause and breaking mountain waves. 01.01.01.02

Exam trap. The layers are defined by temperature behaviour, not by gas composition or pressure. And temperature does not rise through the whole stratosphere: in the ISA it stays at −56.5 °C up to 20 km and only rises above that.

1.2 The troposphere and the tropopause

The troposphere reaches about 8 km (FL 250–300) over the poles, 11 km (36 090 ft) in the ISA mid-latitudes and 16–18 km (around FL 550) over the equator. It contains roughly 75–80 % of the mass of the atmosphere, and about half of the total mass lies below 18 000 ft. Its mean lapse rate is 0.65 °C per 100 m. It is deeper over warm air, because a warm column of air expands, so it is thickest at the equator and in summer. 01.01.02.01

The tropopause acts as a lid on convection: rising cloud reaches the very stable air above and spreads out sideways, which is why a mature Cb flattens into an anvil at tropopause level. An overshooting top that punches above the anvil marks an exceptionally strong updraft. The tropopause is not a continuous surface. It descends in steps at the boundaries of the main air masses, and the strongest winds and most clear-air turbulence concentrate near those breaks, with the maximum wind usually just below the tropopause. Significant weather (SWC) charts plot its height in boxes as flight levels (a box reading 340 means FL 340), with H and L marking local highs and lows of the tropopause surface. 01.01.02.02

By volume, dry air is 78 % nitrogen, 21 % oxygen, 0.93 % argon and about 0.04 % carbon dioxide, plus traces. These proportions stay the same up to about 80 km. Water vapour is extra and very variable, from almost nothing to about 4 % by volume in warm tropical air. Small as it is, water vapour matters more than any other gas to weather: it is the source of all cloud and icing, and the latent heat it carries powers thunderstorms and tropical revolving storms. 01.01.02.03

Exam trap. The percentage of oxygen does not fall with height. What falls is its partial pressure, and that is what causes hypoxia.

Because the equatorial troposphere is so deep and keeps cooling all the way up, the equatorial tropopause is the coldest, at about −75 to −80 °C. The polar tropopause, much lower, sits at about −45 to −55 °C. The rule to remember is high tropopause, cold tropopause. The lowest outside air temperatures on long-haul flights are therefore met at high flight levels in the tropics, which matters for fuel temperature. Tropical Cb tops also reach FL 500 and above, so they cannot be overflown as they often can in mid-latitudes. 01.01.02.04

The steps in the tropopause occur at the subtropical boundary near 30° and at the polar front between about 40° and 60°. Across these boundaries the horizontal temperature contrast is large, and through the thermal wind (explained in Chapter 2) that contrast produces the subtropical jet and the polar front jet. Each jet sits in its break, just below the higher, warm-side tropopause. Flying across a break you may see a sudden change in outside air temperature, strong vertical wind shear and probable CAT. 01.01.02.05

The same expansion of warm air explains seasonal and pressure-related changes. The tropopause is higher in summer and over warm high-pressure systems, and lower in winter and over cold lows and cold upper troughs. Over a deep cold low it can come down to FL 250 or lower, so an aircraft holding a constant cruise level can find itself in the stratosphere: warmer, drier and possibly richer in ozone. 01.01.02.06

Exam trap. "The tropopause is higher over a low" is wrong. It is lower over cold lows and higher over warm highs.

1.3 The stratosphere and ozone

From the tropopause upward the ISA stratosphere is isothermal at −56.5 °C from 11 km (36 090 ft) to 20 km (65 617 ft), then warms by 1 °C per km up to 32 km. Real temperatures vary, and the polar winter stratosphere can warm suddenly. The air is very dry and very stable, the flow is mainly horizontal, and wind speed generally decreases above the jet core. Low density at these levels narrows the margin between high-speed buffet and low-speed buffet (the "coffin corner"). 01.01.03.01

Exam trap. Extrapolating the tropospheric lapse rate gives an ISA temperature at FL 450 of about −75 °C. That is wrong: above 36 090 ft the ISA temperature stays at −56.5 °C.

Ozone concentration increases above the tropopause and peaks at about 20–25 km. At jet cruise levels you meet the most ozone when the tropopause is low: at high latitudes, in winter and spring, and behind cold lows where stratospheric air is drawn down in a tropopause fold. Ozone irritates the eyes, nose and throat and can cause chest pain, coughing, headache and fatigue. Aircraft use catalytic ozone converters, and flight planning can avoid the highest levels at high latitudes in spring; descending is the immediate remedy. 01.01.03.02

1.4 Temperature: definition and units

Air temperature measures the mean kinetic energy of the air molecules. The temperature in a METAR is measured in the shade, in a ventilated screen (the Stevenson screen or an equivalent) 1.25 to 2 m above short grass, so that sunshine and the hot or cold ground do not distort it. It is therefore not the runway surface temperature: after a clear night a runway can be icy while the METAR shows a positive temperature. Outside air temperature drives density altitude, true airspeed, icing risk and engine thrust. 01.02.01.01

Aviation uses three scales. °F = 9/5 × °C + 32, °C = 5/9 × (°F − 32), and K = °C + 273.15. A difference of 1 °C equals 1 K or 1.8 °F. Two checks the exam likes: −40 °C equals −40 °F, and the ISA sea-level temperature of 15 °C is 288.15 K or 59 °F. METARs and TAFs report in °C, with M for minus (M05 is −5 °C); some US products use °F. 01.02.01.02

Exam trap. Temperature is measured at about 1.25–2 m. The 10 m figure belongs to the surface wind.

1.5 How temperature changes with height

In the ISA the temperature is +15 °C at mean sea level and falls by 0.65 °C per 100 m (1.98 °C per 1000 ft) to −56.5 °C at 11 km (36 090 ft). It then stays constant up to 20 km, about FL 650, and rises above that. The real atmosphere has the same shape on average but includes inversions and isothermal layers, and its tropopause height changes with latitude and season. 01.02.02.01

Why does the troposphere get colder with height? The atmosphere lets most incoming sunlight through, so the ground is heated first and passes its heat to the air from below, by conduction, convection, turbulence, latent heat and long-wave radiation. Air higher up is further from this heat source. In addition, air that rises meets lower pressure, expands and cools adiabatically. These two effects together give the negative lapse rate, and they are why there is a freezing level, a cloud base and an icing layer at all. 01.02.02.02

Exam trap. The air does not get colder with height "because it is further from the sun" or "because the air absorbs sunlight directly". The source of heat is the ground.

To find the ISA temperature below the tropopause, use ISA temperature = 15 − 2 × (altitude in thousands of feet); the exact factor is 1.98. Above 36 090 ft it is −56.5 °C. The ISA deviation is the actual temperature minus the ISA temperature at that pressure level. Always use the flight level (the pressure altitude), never the true altitude. 01.02.02.03

Worked example. At FL 180 the outside air temperature is −31 °C. ISA at FL 180 = 15 − 36 = −21 °C. Deviation = −31 − (−21) = ISA −10.

At FL 390 the outside air temperature is −50 °C. ISA above the tropopause = −56.5 °C. Deviation = −50 − (−56.5) = ISA +6.5.

On an upper wind and temperature chart, a route question may ask for the mean ISA deviation. Average the spot temperatures along the route first, then subtract the ISA value for that level.

1.6 How the air gains and loses heat

Heat flows from warmer to colder bodies, and in the atmosphere it moves in six ways: radiation, conduction, convection, advection, turbulence and latent heat. Uneven heating, between land and sea, day and night, or sunlit and shaded slopes, sets up local transfers that produce thermals, breezes and fog. In the exam, match each process to its weather: radiation gives radiation fog, advection gives advection fog, convection gives Cu and Cb, and turbulent mixing is what prevents fog. 01.02.03.01

Radiation is energy carried by electromagnetic waves, which need no medium. Every body radiates according to its temperature: emitted energy rises with the fourth power of absolute temperature (Stefan–Boltzmann law), and the hotter the body, the shorter the wavelength at which it emits most (Wien's law). The sun, at about 6000 K, radiates short-wave energy. The Earth, at about 288 K, radiates long-wave infrared. Short-wave sunlight mostly passes through the air and heats the ground; it does not heat the air directly. 01.02.03.02

Sunlight reaches us as visible light, ultraviolet and near-infrared. Of the energy arriving at the top of the atmosphere, about 30 % is reflected straight back to space by cloud, snow and ice (the albedo), about 20 % is absorbed in the atmosphere by ozone, water vapour and cloud, and about 50 % is absorbed by the surface. How much arrives at a given place depends on the sun's elevation, which changes with latitude, season and time of day. Fresh snow reflects 80–90 % and so stays cold even in sunshine, while daytime heating of bare land drives the afternoon maximum of thermals and Cu or Cb over land. 01.02.03.03

The atmosphere filters sunlight on the way down. Ozone absorbs ultraviolet, which is what warms the stratosphere. Water vapour and CO₂ absorb parts of the near-infrared. Cloud, dust and aerosols reflect and scatter it; the scattering of blue light by air molecules (Rayleigh scattering) is why the sky is blue. In the visible band the air is nearly transparent, an "atmospheric window" for sunlight. Overcast skies reduce daytime heating, so convection is weaker and the daily temperature range smaller. UV exposure grows with altitude because less ozone and air lie above. 01.02.03.04

The Earth's surface radiates long-wave infrared continuously, day and night. By day solar input more than replaces it; at night nothing does, so the surface cools. Night cooling is strongest with clear skies, dry air, light wind and long nights. The minimum temperature usually comes around sunrise, and radiation fog is often thickest just after sunrise. 01.02.03.05

Exam trap. The Earth does not "only radiate at night". It radiates all the time; at night its radiation balance turns negative.

Some of the long-wave radiation leaving the surface never escapes. Water vapour, CO₂, methane, ozone and, above all, cloud absorb it and send part of it back down as counter-radiation. This is the greenhouse effect. In clear, dry air some infrared escapes through a window at around 8–12 µm. That is why humid or cloudy nights stay mild, while dry desert nights cool sharply and the desert has a large daily range. If asked which constituent absorbs terrestrial radiation most effectively, the answer is water vapour, and cloud. 01.02.03.06

Cloud therefore works both ways. By day its tops reflect much of the sunshine and the surface heats less. By night its base absorbs the ground's radiation and radiates it back down, and the surface cools less. An overcast day has a lower maximum, a higher minimum and a small daily range, and an overcast night rarely produces radiation fog; skies clearing in the evening sharply raise the fog risk. Cloud tops themselves cool by radiation at night, which destabilises the cloud layer and explains why thunderstorms over the ocean peak at night. 01.02.03.07

Conduction is heat transfer by molecular contact, without the air itself moving. Air conducts heat very poorly, so conduction only affects the lowest centimetres to metres of air touching the ground. It starts the process; convection and turbulence spread the heat further. 01.02.03.08

The ground warms or chills the thin layer of air in contact with it, and that layer's heat is then carried upward by turbulence (if there is wind) or by convection (if the air is unstable). In calm conditions the effect stays in a shallow layer, which is how strong surface inversions form at night. A calm, clear night gives shallow, intense cooling: shallow radiation fog and ground frost. A wind of 5–10 kt spreads the cooling through a deeper layer, so fog is thicker or lifts into low stratus; a stronger wind prevents fog altogether. 01.02.03.09

Convection is vertical heat transport by bulk motion of the air. Air heated from below becomes warmer and less dense than its surroundings and rises as thermals, while cooler air sinks to replace it. Convection is efficient only when the air is unstable (Chapter 3). Its signatures are Cu, towering Cu (TCU) and Cb, showers, thermal turbulence below cloud base, and good visibility, because pollution is mixed upward and away. In meteorology convection always means vertical motion and advection horizontal motion. 01.02.03.10

Convection occurs when the land is strongly heated by day, especially on summer afternoons; when cold air moves over a warmer surface, as with polar air over a warm sea in winter and at night; when conditionally unstable air is lifted at fronts, convergence lines or mountains (forced convection); and when cloud tops cool at night. Over land the convective maximum is in the afternoon, over the sea at night and early morning. Winter showers on west- and north-facing coasts come from polar air crossing the relatively warm sea. 01.02.03.11

Advection is horizontal transport, by the wind, of the air's properties such as heat and moisture. Warm advection raises the temperature at a place and cold advection lowers it. Seen in the vertical, warm advection makes the wind veer with height in the northern hemisphere and cold advection makes it back. Warm, moist air advected over a cold ground or sea gives advection fog, which unlike radiation fog can form in wind and at any time of day. Cold air advected over a warm surface becomes unstable and produces showers. 01.02.03.12

Advection happens whenever air masses move: with fronts, with air crossing between land and sea (sea breezes and onshore winds) and with large-scale flow from one source region to another, such as tropical maritime air reaching Europe in winter. At coastal airports an onshore wind shift can bring sea fog in within minutes, and in winter a warm sector of tropical maritime air over a cold continent produces widespread advection fog and low stratus. 01.02.03.13

Turbulence is mechanical eddying caused by wind blowing over rough ground or by wind shear. The eddies mix the air vertically through the friction layer, roughly the lowest 1000–3000 ft, carrying heat, moisture and momentum. They lift surface cooling to higher levels and bring faster-moving air down to the surface. In moist air, turbulent mixing produces a turbulence inversion at the top of the mixed layer, with stratus or stratocumulus beneath it. A night wind above about 10–15 kt usually prevents radiation fog and gives low stratus instead. 01.02.03.14

Latent heat is the energy hidden in a change of state. Evaporation takes about 2500 J per gram of water from the surroundings, and condensation gives the same amount back to the air. Water vapour therefore carries energy from the warm surface, mostly the oceans, to wherever it condenses aloft. Freezing releases about 334 J/g, and the direct change from vapour to ice (deposition) about 2834 J/g. The release of latent heat in condensing cloud is the fuel of Cb and tropical revolving storms, and it is why saturated air cools more slowly when it rises than dry air does (Chapter 3). The reverse matters too: rain evaporating into dry air cools that air, makes it dense and drives downbursts and microbursts under virga. 01.02.03.15

1.7 Lapse rates

The environmental lapse rate (ELR) is the actual fall of temperature with height in the air around you, as measured by a sounding. Its mean value is 0.65 °C per 100 m, which is 1.98, or about 2 °C per 1000 ft. Actual values vary widely: steeper than 1 °C per 100 m just above a heated surface, zero in an isothermal layer and negative in an inversion. Keep the ELR separate from the two adiabatic rates, which describe a parcel of air that is moving vertically: the dry adiabatic lapse rate (DALR) of 1 °C per 100 m (3 °C per 1000 ft) and the saturated adiabatic lapse rate (SALR) of about 0.6 °C per 100 m (1.8 °C per 1000 ft) near the surface. A quick estimate of the freezing level above the ground is the surface temperature divided by 2, in thousands of feet: +12 °C at the surface gives a freezing level near 6000 ft above ground. 01.02.04.01

Exam trap. The ELR is a property of the environment. The DALR and SALR are properties of a moving parcel. An answer that quotes the ISA lapse rate as 3 °C per 1000 ft has confused it with the DALR.

1.8 Inversions

An inversion is a layer in which temperature increases with height; an isothermal layer is one in which it stays constant. They form in three ways: cooling from below (by radiation or advection), warming from above (by subsiding air), or one air mass lying over another (at a front). The types are the ground (radiation) inversion, the advection inversion, the subsidence inversion, the frontal inversion, the turbulence inversion at the top of the friction layer, the valley inversion, and the tropopause itself. Inversions trap haze, smoke and fog beneath them, and on climb or approach you can expect wind shear and turbulence at their top. 01.02.05.01

Both inversions and isothermal layers are absolutely stable. A parcel lifted into one cools at the DALR or SALR while the air around it stays as warm or gets warmer, so the parcel is always colder and denser than its surroundings and sinks back. Vertical motion is suppressed and convection stops at the inversion base. A stable layer therefore means stratiform cloud with flat tops, smooth air above, and haze and poor visibility below. 01.02.05.02

Exam trap. An isothermal layer is not "neutral". Its lapse rate (zero) is less than the SALR, so it is stable.

Each inversion has its own cause:

  • A nocturnal radiation inversion forms when the ground cools on a clear, calm night and chills the air above it. It is shallow and breaks up with morning heating.
  • An advection inversion forms when warm air flows over a cold surface and is cooled from below.
  • A subsidence inversion forms when air sinking in a high-pressure system warms at the DALR and ends up warmer than the air beneath it. It typically lies at 3000–6000 ft and is persistent. It caps stratocumulus and haze in anticyclones, giving the dull, grey "anticyclonic gloom".
  • A frontal inversion forms where warm air overlies the cold wedge of air at a front, so it slopes with the frontal surface. Rain falling from the warm air into sub-zero air beneath produces freezing rain.
  • A turbulence inversion forms above the friction layer. Mixing gives the lowest layer a DALR profile, so its top ends up colder than the undisturbed air above.
  • A valley inversion forms when cold air drains into a valley at night (a katabatic flow) and pools under warmer air. It traps fog and pollution in the valley and brings wind shear at its top.

01.02.05.03

1.9 Temperature near the surface

The surface temperature follows its radiation balance: positive by day, when absorbed sunlight exceeds emitted infrared, and negative at night. Land has a low heat capacity and passes little heat down into the ground, so it heats and cools quickly. Water has a high heat capacity, mixes, and loses heat by evaporation, so the sea surface temperature changes by less than about 1 °C in a day. Because the balance stays positive for a while after noon, the maximum air temperature comes 1–2 hours after local noon; the minimum comes around sunrise. This land–sea contrast drives sea and land breezes and, on the largest scale, the monsoons. 01.02.06.01

The air in contact with the surface gains or loses heat by conduction, and turbulence spreads it through the friction layer. Over the sea the air temperature follows the sea temperature closely, so its daily variation is small. The daily range is largest over dry inland deserts and smallest over the oceans. Afternoon mixing also brings stronger wind down, which is why surface winds are often gusty by day and calm at night. 01.02.06.02

Cloud reflects sunshine by day, lowering the maximum, and returns long-wave radiation at night, raising the minimum. Low, thick water cloud has the strongest effect; thin high cirrus the weakest. An overcast sky reduces the daily temperature range. For fog forecasting, evening clearing plus moist air plus light wind means a high risk. 01.02.06.03

Wind creates turbulence that spreads surface heating or cooling through a deeper layer, so the air near the ground changes temperature less. Calm air allows extreme surface temperatures and strong inversions. A calm, clear night gives the lowest minima, ground frost and shallow fog; a moderate wind gives a milder night with low stratus instead of fog; and a strong daytime wind lowers the maximum by mixing. 01.02.06.04

1.10 Pressure

Atmospheric pressure is the force per unit area exerted by the weight of the column of air above a point. Static pressure acts equally in all directions. The ISA mean sea level value is 1013.25 hPa, which equals 29.92 inHg or 760 mmHg. Pressure always decreases with height, because there is less air above; it never inverts the way temperature can. It is the quantity behind altimetry and the pitot-static instruments (altimeter, ASI and VSI). 01.03.01.01

Europe uses hectopascals (1 hPa = 1 mbar = 100 Pa); the USA and Canada use inches of mercury. 1013.25 hPa = 29.92 inHg, 1 inHg is about 33.86 hPa and 1 hPa about 0.0295 inHg. Mixing them up is dangerous: setting 29.92 inHg as "992 hPa" puts the altimeter about 21 × 30 = 640 ft out. 01.03.01.02

A mercury barometer balances the weight of the air pressing on an open reservoir against a column of mercury in an evacuated tube; at 1013 hPa the column stands about 760 mm high. Its readings need corrections for temperature, gravity and the barometer's height. An aneroid barometer uses a sealed, partly evacuated metal capsule that expands or contracts as pressure changes, moving a pointer through a linkage. A barograph is a recording aneroid that shows the pressure tendency. The aircraft altimeter is simply an aneroid barometer graduated in feet according to the ISA, which is the root of every temperature error in section 1.14. 01.03.01.03

On surface charts, isobars join points of equal QFF, that is pressure reduced to mean sea level. They are usually drawn every 4 hPa (sometimes 5 or 2 hPa). Their spacing shows the pressure gradient: closely spaced isobars mean a strong gradient and a strong wind. In chart questions, the wind blows roughly along the isobars with low pressure on the left in the northern hemisphere, slightly backed and slower near the surface because of friction (Chapter 2), and stronger where isobars are closer. 01.03.01.04

Exam trap. Isobars on a surface chart are drawn from QFF, not QNH.

The shapes on a pressure chart have names:

  • A high, or anticyclone, has closed isobars with the highest pressure in the centre. Air circulates clockwise around it in the northern hemisphere, diverges at the surface and subsides.
  • A low, also called a depression or cyclone, has closed isobars with the lowest pressure in the centre. Air circulates anticlockwise in the northern hemisphere, converges at the surface and rises.
  • A trough is an elongated extension of low pressure with V-shaped isobars. Air converges there, often with showers or a front, and the wind veers as it passes.
  • A ridge is an elongated extension of high pressure with U-shaped isobars and generally fair weather.
  • A col is the saddle between two highs and two lows. Its gradient is slack and its winds light and variable, so it brings fog in autumn and winter and thunderstorms in summer.

01.03.01.05

1.11 Pressure and height

Pressure falls with height according to the hydrostatic equation, dP = −ρ g dh: the fall over a layer equals the weight of the air in it. Since density decreases with height, each hectopascal corresponds to more height the higher you go, and pressure falls roughly exponentially. In cold, dense air pressure falls faster with height than in warm air, so the thickness between two pressure levels is proportional to the mean temperature of the layer. A given pressure level therefore lies lower in cold air, which is the root cause of the rule that cold air puts you lower than indicated. On upper-air charts, contours (isohypses) show the height of a pressure surface, and low heights mean cold air and low pressure aloft. 01.03.02.01

Near mean sea level, 1 hPa corresponds to about 27–30 ft (8–9 m); the exam uses 30 ft per hPa. This barometric lapse rate grows with height, to about 50 ft per hPa at 18 000 ft, 70 ft per hPa at FL 300 and over 100 ft per hPa at FL 400, and it is larger in warmer air. It gives the quick conversion QNH = QFE + elevation ÷ 30, with elevation in feet and the result in hectopascals. Do not use 30 ft per hPa at high altitude. 01.03.02.02

In the ISA the pressure at 18 000 ft (FL 180) is about 500 hPa, half its sea-level value. Density falls more slowly than pressure, because the temperature is falling too (ρ = P / RT), so half the sea-level density is reached higher, at about 22 000 ft, and a quarter at about 40 000 ft. Lower density means a true airspeed higher than the indicated airspeed, less engine thrust or power, and a hypoxia risk. 01.03.02.03

1.12 QFF and surface charts

QFF is the station pressure (QFE) reduced to mean sea level using the actual temperature (and humidity) at the station, assumed to fill an imaginary column of air between station level and sea level. It is the pressure used for synoptic charts. QNH is reduced using ISA conditions instead, so QFF and QNH are generally not equal. 01.03.03.01

To reduce QFE to QFF, the meteorologist adds the weight of that imaginary column, worked out with the actual station temperature. A cold column is denser and heavier, so the correction is larger. For a station above sea level it follows that QFF is higher than QNH when the air is colder than ISA, lower when it is warmer, and equal in ISA conditions. For a station at sea level QFE, QNH and QFF are all the same. 01.03.03.02

Worked example. An aerodrome at 1000 ft reports QNH 1010 hPa with a temperature of ISA −15. Is QFF higher or lower than 1010? The real column is colder than ISA and so heavier, so the reduction adds more than the ISA reduction did: QFF is greater than 1010 hPa.

Reducing every station to sea level removes the effect of elevation, so the pressure at stations at different heights can be compared and isobars drawn between them. That is why surface analyses use QFF. Pilots still set QNH, never QFF. 01.03.03.03

1.13 Surface systems and systems aloft

Whether a surface high or low persists with height depends on the temperature of the air column, because the thickness of a layer is proportional to its mean temperature. In a cold low (the cold core of a mature depression or an upper trough), isobaric surfaces sag more and more with height, so the low becomes deeper aloft. In a warm high (a subtropical or blocking high), the surfaces bulge more with height, so the high strengthens aloft. Cold lows and warm highs are the systems that extend to great heights. A warm, thermal low is low at the surface, but its warm column lifts the surfaces above it, so it weakens with height and becomes a high aloft; it is shallow. A cold high, such as the Siberian winter high, is high at the surface but low aloft, and is also shallow. Shallow systems like the summer thermal low over Iberia or the Siberian high do not appear on a 300 hPa chart. Upper-level systems steer the surface ones, so always read the upper-air charts together with the surface chart. 01.03.04.01

1.14 Density

Pressure, temperature and density are linked by the equation of state for an ideal gas, P = ρ R T, where R is 287 J/kg·K for dry air and T is in kelvin. At constant pressure density is inversely proportional to absolute temperature; at constant temperature it is proportional to pressure. Moisture lowers density, because water vapour molecules are lighter than nitrogen and oxygen molecules. The lowest density, and so the highest density altitude, comes with a high, hot, humid aerodrome and low pressure: a longer take-off run, a poorer climb gradient and less engine output. Always use kelvin in ratio calculations. 01.04.01.01

Density decreases with height, but more slowly than pressure because falling temperature partly offsets the falling pressure. In the ISA it is 1.225 kg/m³ at sea level, about half that at 22 000 ft and a quarter at 40 000 ft. Above the tropopause, where temperature is constant, density falls at the same rate as pressure. This is why true airspeed rises with altitude at constant indicated airspeed, why engine thrust falls, and why buffet margins narrow at high levels. Warm air at a given pressure altitude has a lower density and therefore a higher density altitude. 01.04.01.02

1.15 The International Standard Atmosphere

The ICAO Standard Atmosphere (ISA) is a model atmosphere: dry, still air with fixed sea-level values and fixed lapse rates, roughly matching the annual mean at mid-latitudes. It is not the average at any particular place. It gives a common reference for calibrating pressure instruments (altimeter, ASI, VSI), for defining pressure altitude and flight levels, and for presenting aircraft performance, which is then corrected for the actual conditions, expressed as "ISA ±". Performance charts are entered with pressure altitude and either the ISA deviation or the OAT. 01.05.01.01

Isothermal layer −56.5 °C from 11 to 20 km (≈ 65 600 ft)
Above 20 km +1 °C/km to 32 km
850 hPa ≈ 4 780 ft (≈ FL 050)
700 hPa ≈ 9 880 ft (≈ FL 100)
500 hPa ≈ 18 280 ft (≈ FL 180)
300 hPa ≈ 30 070 ft (≈ FL 300)
250 hPa ≈ 34 000 ft (≈ FL 340)
200 hPa ≈ 38 660 ft (≈ FL 390)

01.05.01.02

The pressure-level heights are what you need to read upper-air charts: a 300 hPa chart describes conditions near FL 300.

Exam trap. The ISA tropopause is at 11 km, which is 36 090 ft. It is not at 11 000 ft, and not exactly at FL 360. The ISA lapse rate is about 2 °C per 1000 ft; 3 °C per 1000 ft is the DALR.

1.16 Altimetry: the vocabulary

Altimetry questions are mostly about choosing the right reference. These terms are defined by ICAO:

  • Height is the vertical distance of a level, point or object above a specified datum, such as the ground or the aerodrome (read on QFE).
  • Altitude is the vertical distance above mean sea level (read on QNH).
  • Elevation is the vertical distance of a point on the Earth's surface above mean sea level.
  • Pressure altitude is the altitude in the ISA that matches the pressure at a point. It is what the altimeter reads with 1013.25 hPa set.
  • A flight level is a surface of constant pressure related to 1013.25 hPa, separated from others by set intervals. The FL number is the pressure altitude divided by 100.
  • A pressure level is any surface of constant pressure, such as 500 hPa.
  • True altitude and true height are the real, geometric distances above sea level and above the ground.
  • QNH is the setting that makes the altimeter read aerodrome elevation on the ground; it is QFE reduced to sea level using ISA. QFE is the pressure at aerodrome (or threshold) level, with which the altimeter reads zero on the ground. The standard setting is 1013.25 hPa.

Indicated altitude on QNH equals true altitude only in ISA conditions, and on the ground at the aerodrome. A flight level is a pressure surface, not a fixed height above sea level: its true height changes with pressure and temperature. 01.06.01.01

The transition altitude (TA) is the altitude at or below which an aircraft's vertical position is given as altitude, on QNH. The transition level (TL) is the lowest flight level available above the transition altitude; it changes with QNH (and temperature), and a low QNH gives a higher TL. Between them lies the transition layer, where no level flight takes place. Terrain clearance is the true vertical distance between aircraft and terrain, and the lowest usable flight level is the lowest flight level that still gives the required terrain clearance in the actual pressure and temperature. Low pressure and cold air both raise the lowest usable flight level. 01.06.01.02

1.17 Altimeter settings and procedures

Each setting goes with one reference: QFE gives height above the aerodrome or threshold, QNH gives altitude, and 1013.25 hPa gives pressure altitude and so the flight level. Some states also use a regional QNH, the lowest forecast QNH in a region, for safe altitudes en route. Decision altitudes and minimum descent altitudes are published on QNH; decision heights and minimum descent heights relate to QFE or the radio altimeter. 01.06.02.01

Below the transition altitude, set the QNH of the nearest aerodrome or the regional QNH. At or above the transition level, set 1013.25 hPa. On a climb you change from QNH to standard as you pass the transition altitude; on descent you change from standard to QNH as you pass the transition level, once cleared to an altitude. In the transition layer, report your level as a flight level when climbing and as an altitude when descending. Before take-off, check the altimeter on QNH against the known aerodrome elevation. 01.06.02.02

An error of 1 hPa in the setting gives about 30 ft of error in the reading. The direction is easy to remember: subscale up, reading up. If the QNH set is too high, the altimeter over-reads and the aircraft is lower than indicated, which is the controlled-flight-into-terrain risk.

1.18 Altimeter calculations

Near sea level the reading changes by about 30 ft for each hectopascal the setting changes. Raise the subscale by x hPa and the reading rises by about 30x ft. 01.06.03.01

Worked example · changing the setting. An aircraft flies at 3000 ft on QNH 1003 hPa. With 1013 set, it reads 3000 + (1013 − 1003) × 30 = 3300 ft, FL 033. The aerodrome elevation is 600 ft, so QFE = 1003 − 600 ÷ 30 = 983 hPa, and on QFE the altimeter reads 3000 − 600 = 2400 ft.

The most common error is the sign. With a low QNH, pressure altitude is higher than altitude. For any aerodrome above sea level, QFE is lower than QNH.

Worked example · through TA and TL. The transition altitude is 5000 ft and QNH is 993 hPa. Climbing through 5000 ft on QNH, the pilot sets 1013: the reading jumps to 5000 + 20 × 30 = 5600 ft (FL 056), though the aircraft has not moved. Descending, with a transition level of FL 070, the pilot sets QNH 993 at FL 070 and the reading drops to 7000 − 600 = 6400 ft.

With QNH below 1013 the reading increases when 1013 is set; with QNH above 1013 it decreases. The transition level must keep a buffer above the transition altitude, so a low QNH means a higher TL.

01.06.03.02

On the ground at the aerodrome, the altimeter reads zero on QFE, the elevation on QNH, and the pressure altitude on 1013.25 hPa, where pressure altitude = elevation + (1013 − QNH) × 30 ft. For example, at an elevation of 1500 ft with QNH 1023 hPa, 1013 set reads 1500 − 300 = 1200 ft. A high QNH gives a pressure altitude below the elevation, and so better performance. Before flight, the reading on QNH should be within the tolerance given in the aircraft manual, typically about ±60 ft. 01.06.03.03

1.19 Temperature, pressure and true altitude

The altimeter assumes the ISA temperature. In air colder than ISA the column is denser, pressure falls faster with height, and the pressure levels are lower and closer together. You are lower than the altimeter shows, and two aircraft separated by 1000 ft in flight level are in fact less than 1000 ft apart. Warmer air does the opposite. The exam's rule is that the error is about 4 % of the height above the setting datum for every 10 °C of ISA deviation. Measure it from the level of the station that supplied the setting, which on QNH or QFE is the aerodrome elevation, and where a question gives terrain heights, read carefully which reference it intends. In very cold weather, cold-temperature corrections are added to minimum altitudes such as the decision altitude, the minimum descent altitude and step-down fixes. 01.06.03.04

Pressure does the same thing. If you fly at a constant indicated altitude without updating the QNH, you are following a constant pressure surface, and towards a low that surface descends, by about 30 ft per hPa. Flying towards lower pressure, your true altitude falls; towards higher pressure, it rises. Both effects are captured in one phrase: from high to low, look out below. 01.06.03.05

Worked example · pressure. An aircraft cruises at a constant flight level from A (QNH 1030 hPa) to B (QNH 990 hPa). The 40 hPa difference is about 40 × 30 = 1200 ft, so the aircraft is about 1200 ft lower in true altitude over B. In the northern hemisphere, a drift to the right (wind from the left) means you are heading towards lower pressure, and so lower than indicated.

The 4 % rule is the same as 4 ft per 1000 ft per °C. To find true altitude, add ISA deviation × 4 × (height above the datum ÷ 1000) to the indicated value; with a negative deviation this subtracts. Use the deviation of the mean temperature of the column if the question gives it. 01.06.03.06

Worked example · temperature. An aircraft indicates 9000 ft on QNH at an aerodrome with an elevation of 1000 ft, in ISA −15. Height above the aerodrome is about 8000 ft. The correction is −15 × 4 × 8 = −480 ft, so the true altitude is about 8520 ft.

To find terrain clearance, first allow for pressure, then for temperature, then subtract the terrain. At a flight level, the true height in ISA temperature is FL × 100 − (1013 − QNH) × 30. Then apply 4 % per 10 °C, then subtract the elevation of the terrain. Low QNH and cold air both reduce clearance, and they add together. 01.06.03.07

Worked example · terrain clearance. An aircraft flies FL 080 over terrain 5000 ft high. QNH is 998 hPa and the temperature is ISA −10.

  1. Pressure: 8000 − (1013 − 998) × 30 = 8000 − 450 = 7550 ft.
  2. Temperature: 4 % of 7550 is about 300 ft, so about 7250 ft.
  3. Terrain: 7250 − 5000 = about 2250 ft clearance.

The 4 % rule is not exact, but it can be used in either direction: to find true altitude from indicated altitude or indicated altitude from true. The small error this introduces is acceptable in the exam. Apply it to the height above the setting datum, then add the elevation of the datum. 01.06.03.08

1.20 Wind over mountains and the altimeter

Wind accelerating over a ridge or through a gap (the Venturi effect) has a lower static pressure, by Bernoulli's law, p + ½ρv² = constant. The altimeter senses that lower pressure and over-reads, so the aircraft is lower than indicated, and the error is greatest right next to the terrain causing it. Combined with cold air and the downdrafts of mountain waves (Chapter 2), the error can reach several hundred feet, or more than 1000 ft. In strong winds across mountains, add a margin to minimum safe altitudes and cross ridges well above them. 01.06.04.01

Exam trap. In accelerated flow the altimeter over-reads. It does not under-read.

Check yourself

  1. Where is the tropopause coldest, and why? Over the equator, at about −75 to −80 °C. The equatorial troposphere is deepest, so the air keeps cooling to a much greater height.
  2. At FL 280 the outside air temperature is −35 °C. What is the ISA deviation? ISA at FL 280 is 15 − 56 = −41 °C. −35 − (−41) = ISA +6.
  3. An aerodrome at 1500 ft reports QNH 1001 hPa with the air much colder than ISA. Is QFF above or below 1001? Above. The cold, heavy imaginary column adds more pressure than the ISA reduction did.
  4. You fly FL 060 with QNH 983 hPa and ISA −20 over a ridge of 4000 ft. Roughly what is your clearance? Pressure: 6000 − 30 × 30 = 5100 ft. Temperature: 8 % of 5100 ≈ 400 ft, so about 4700 ft. Clearance about 700 ft.
  5. Which two kinds of pressure system extend to great heights? Cold lows and warm highs.
  6. Is an isothermal layer stable, neutral or unstable? Absolutely stable: its lapse rate (zero) is below both the SALR and the DALR.
  7. A runway shows +2 °C in the METAR after a clear, calm night. Can it be icy? Yes. The METAR temperature is measured at 1.25–2 m; the surface itself can be well below zero after strong radiative cooling.

2.17 Where the jet sits, and where the CAT is

chapters.html:
Wind is air moving from high towards low pressure, bent by the Earth's rotation, slowed by friction and curved around pressure systems. This chapter builds the wind up from those forces, then follows it down into the friction layer, out into the global circulation, into local winds and mountain waves, and up to the jet streams and the clear-air turbulence they carry.

2.1 What wind is and how it is reported

Wind is the horizontal movement of air relative to the Earth's surface. It is always given by the direction it blows from and its speed, so 270/20 is a 20 kt wind from the west. Vertical movements are called updrafts and downdrafts, not wind. The surface wind is the wind measured 10 m above open, level ground. It decides the runway in use, the crosswind and tailwind components, and the take-off and landing distances. 02.01.01.01

Wind directions are given in degrees true in METARs, TAFs, SIGMETs, upper-wind charts and other written reports, and in degrees magnetic when the tower or ATIS gives a wind for runway use. Speeds are in knots (KT) or metres per second (MPS); 1 m/s is about 2 kt, and some charts use km/h. To work out a crosswind from a METAR, first convert its true direction to magnetic with the local variation, then compare it with the runway's magnetic heading. 02.01.01.02

Exam trap. The ATIS and tower wind is magnetic, not true.

The reported wind is an average from an anemometer and wind vane at 10 m. The tower (and any ATS unit or local report) averages over 2 minutes; METARs and SPECIs average over 10 minutes, unless there was a marked discontinuity, in which case only the period after it is used. A gust is the highest 3-second mean wind, reported when it exceeds the mean by 10 kt or more. The direction is reported as VRB when the mean speed is 3 kt or less (or the direction varies widely), and in the form "dddVddd" when it varies by 60° or more with a mean of 3 kt or more. The 2-minute tower wind describes conditions at landing better than the 10-minute METAR wind. 02.01.01.03

2.2 The pressure gradient force

The horizontal pressure gradient is how fast pressure changes with horizontal distance, measured at right angles to the isobars from high to low (in hPa per 100 km, say). Closely spaced isobars mean a strong gradient. 02.02.01.01

The gradient produces the pressure gradient force (PGF), which per unit mass is (1/ρ) × ΔP/Δn. It acts from high to low pressure, at right angles to the isobars, and it is what sets the air moving. Because density appears underneath, the same pressure difference produces a larger force where the air is thinner; that, plus the absence of friction, is why the same isobar spacing gives a stronger wind aloft than at the surface. 02.02.01.02

Exam trap. The pressure gradient force acts at right angles to the isobars, never along them.

2.3 The Coriolis force

As soon as air moves, the Earth turns beneath it, and to an observer on the ground the air appears deflected. This apparent force is the Coriolis force, CF = 2 Ω V sin φ, where Ω is the Earth's rate of rotation, V the wind speed and φ the latitude. It acts at right angles to the motion: to the right in the northern hemisphere and to the left in the southern. It is zero at the equator, greatest at the poles, and proportional to the wind speed. It changes the direction of the air, never its speed, and it cannot start air moving: with no wind there is no Coriolis force. 02.02.01.03

Exam trap. Coriolis is zero at the equator and maximum at the poles, not the other way round.

2.4 The geostrophic wind

Imagine air at rest between a high and a low. The pressure gradient force starts it moving towards the low. As it gains speed, the Coriolis force grows and turns it to the right (northern hemisphere), until the Coriolis force exactly balances the pressure gradient force. The air then flows steadily, without acceleration, parallel to the straight isobars. This is the geostrophic wind, with speed Vg = (ΔP/Δn) ÷ (ρ × 2Ω sin φ). It exists only above the friction layer, with straight, parallel isobars, in steady flow, and more than about 15° from the equator. 02.02.01.04

The geostrophic wind blows along the isobars on surface charts and along the contours on upper-air charts. Buys Ballot's law puts this in a sentence: in the northern hemisphere, stand with your back to the wind and low pressure is on your left; in the southern hemisphere it is on your right. Air therefore circulates anticlockwise round lows and clockwise round highs in the northern hemisphere, and the opposite way in the southern. To find the wind direction at a point on a northern-hemisphere chart, draw the tangent to the isobar with the low on your left. One consequence for altimetry: in the northern hemisphere, a drift to the right means the wind is from the left, so you are flying towards lower pressure and the altimeter over-reads. 02.02.01.05

Exam trap. In a figure showing geostrophic balance, the PGF and Coriolis arrows point the same way in both hemispheres: PGF at the LOW, Coriolis at the HIGH. Only the wind arrow tells you which hemisphere it is. If the LOW is on the wind's right, it is the southern hemisphere.

Latitude changes the geostrophic wind even when the isobar spacing does not. The pressure gradient force depends only on the spacing (and density), but the Coriolis force, 2Ω V sin φ, produces less force per knot of wind the closer you are to the equator, because sin φ shrinks. The wind therefore has to blow faster at low latitudes before its Coriolis force grows big enough to balance the same pressure gradient force: Vg ∝ 1/sin φ. With the spacing that gives 20 kt at 60°, you get about 24 kt at 45° and 35 kt at 30° (sin 60° ÷ sin 30° ≈ 1.7). Turned round, to give the same wind, isobars at low latitude must be further apart, which is why a chart's geostrophic wind scale is drawn for one latitude. Within about 15° of the equator sin φ is so small that the Coriolis force can never catch up: the balance never forms, the air flows straight across the isobars from high to low and fills the pressure difference. Tropical pressure gradients are therefore weak, and tropical charts use streamlines instead of isobars. 02.02.01.06

Exam trap. The same isobar spacing does not give the same wind at all latitudes. Compare spacing only at the same latitude.

2.5 The gradient wind

When the isobars are curved, the air is following a curved path, and that needs a net force towards the centre of the curve. Round a low, the pressure gradient force points inward, while the Coriolis and centrifugal forces point outward: PGF = Coriolis + centrifugal, so the Coriolis force, and with it the wind speed, is smaller than geostrophic. The gradient wind round a low is sub-geostrophic. Round a high, the Coriolis force points inward and balances both the outward pressure gradient force and the centrifugal force, so it must be larger than geostrophic, and the gradient wind round a high is super-geostrophic. For identical spacing and latitude, then, the wind is strongest round a high, middling with straight isobars and weakest round a low. In practice highs usually have weak gradients, so their winds are lighter anyway. 02.02.01.07

2.6 Wind in the friction layer

Near the ground, friction slows the air. The Coriolis force, which depends on speed, weakens with it, so the pressure gradient force is no longer fully balanced and the wind turns across the isobars towards low pressure. Going up, friction decreases, so the wind speeds up and turns until, at the top of the friction layer around 2000–3000 ft, it is geostrophic. In the northern hemisphere the wind therefore veers and increases with height through the friction layer; in the southern hemisphere it backs and increases. On a northern-hemisphere climb-out the wind veers and strengthens; on the descent it backs and weakens, so expect the crosswind and headwind to change on final. 02.02.02.01

The surface wind has a daily cycle. By day, surface heating creates turbulence that mixes the faster, veered air from higher up down to the surface, so the surface wind becomes stronger, veered and gusty, peaking in the early afternoon. At night a surface inversion cuts the surface layer off from the air above, so the surface wind becomes lighter and backed, while the wind just above the inversion may strengthen into a low-level jet (section 2.12). A calm night at the surface with a strong wind at 1000–2000 ft means low-level wind shear on the approach. Over the sea the daily cycle is small. 02.02.02.02

How deep the friction layer is depends on three things: terrain roughness, wind speed and stability. Rough ground, strong wind and unstable air mix momentum higher and give a deeper layer; a smooth surface such as the sea, light wind and stable air (a night inversion) give a shallower one. Typical depths run from about 1000 ft over a calm sea at night to 3000 ft or more over rough ground on an unstable day. 02.02.02.03

For the exam, use these values for the surface wind compared with the geostrophic wind above:

Key numbers · surface wind vs geostrophic wind

Surface Speed Angle across isobars, towards low
Over water ≈ 70 % ≈ 10°
Over land ≈ 50 % ≈ 30°

In the northern hemisphere the surface wind is backed from the 2000 ft wind; in the southern hemisphere it is veered.

Worked example. The 2000 ft wind over land in the northern hemisphere is 270/40. The surface wind is backed by about 30° and halved: about 240/20. Over the sea it is backed about 10° and reduced to 70 %: about 260/28. In the southern hemisphere the same 2000 ft wind over land would give about 300/20.

02.02.02.04

Exam trap. In the northern hemisphere the surface wind is backed relative to the wind aloft. An answer that veers it is the southern-hemisphere case.

2.7 Convergence and divergence

Convergence is a net horizontal inflow of air into a region, so that air piles up; divergence is a net outflow. Air cannot pile up indefinitely, so low-level convergence must be balanced by rising air and divergence aloft, and low-level divergence by sinking air and convergence aloft. Low-level convergence in troughs, the ITCZ or along a sea-breeze front therefore means ascent, cloud and showers. 02.02.03.01

This links the surface to the upper air. In a surface low, friction makes the surface wind cross the isobars inward, so air converges, rises and diverges aloft. If the divergence aloft removes air faster than the surface convergence brings it in, the surface pressure falls and the low deepens. In a surface high, air diverges at the surface, subsides and converges aloft; if the upper convergence exceeds the surface divergence, the high builds. Changes of wind speed along the upper flow, especially at the entrances and exits of jet streams, are what create this upper divergence and convergence, and so develop the surface systems. The weather follows: lows and troughs bring cloud and precipitation; highs bring subsidence, clear skies or a layer of stratiform cloud under an inversion, and haze or fog. 02.02.03.02

Exam trap. A surface low deepens because upper-level divergence exceeds low-level convergence, not because of more surface convergence alone.

2.8 The general circulation

The equator receives more energy than it radiates away and the poles less, so heat must be carried towards the poles. On a non-rotating Earth one giant convection cell per hemisphere would do it. The Earth's rotation breaks it into three cells in each hemisphere:

  • The Hadley cell, from 0° to 30°. Air rises at the equator in the ITCZ, flows poleward aloft, sinks at about 30° into the subtropical highs and returns towards the equator at the surface as the trade winds. It is thermally direct: warm air rises and cool air sinks.
  • The Ferrel cell, from 30° to 60°. At the surface the flow is poleward and deflected into the westerlies; the air rises at about 60°, at the subpolar lows and the polar front. It is thermally indirect: it rises over colder air and sinks over warmer air.
  • The polar cell, from 60° to 90°. Air sinks at the pole into the polar high, flows out at the surface as the polar easterlies and rises at about 60°.

The result is a set of surface pressure belts: the equatorial low, the subtropical highs (the "horse latitudes"), the subpolar lows and the polar highs. Aloft, the flow is mostly westerly from about 20° poleward, with the subtropical and polar front jets embedded in it. 02.03.01.01

The real surface pattern follows the model: the equatorial trough and ITCZ; the north-east trades in the northern hemisphere and south-east trades in the southern; the subtropical highs (Azores, North Pacific, St Helena, Mascarene, South Pacific); the westerlies; the subpolar lows (Icelandic, Aleutian); and the polar easterlies. The whole pattern moves with the sun. In January the belts are shifted south, strong cold highs sit over the continents (the Siberian and North American highs), the Icelandic and Aleutian lows are deep, and the north-east monsoon blows over South Asia. In July the belts are shifted north, a thermal low sits over South Asia (the Pakistan low), the south-west monsoon blows, and the Azores high extends towards Europe. On map questions, the Siberian high belongs only to winter and the Asian low only to summer. Chapter 8 develops this into climatology, including the seasonal movement of the ITCZ. 02.03.01.02

Aloft, westerlies dominate from about 20–30° poleward in both hemispheres and are strongest in winter, when the temperature contrast between pole and equator is greatest. Easterlies blow aloft over the tropics, reaching further from the equator in the summer hemisphere, and in the northern summer the Tropical Easterly Jet blows at about FL 450–500 over South Asia and Africa. Eastbound North Atlantic flights use the westerly tailwind, especially in winter; westbound tracks avoid the jet core. 02.03.01.03

Exam trap. The mid-latitude upper westerlies do not turn easterly in summer. They persist, only weaker.

2.9 Slope and valley winds

On a sunny day a mountain slope heats the air in contact with it, which becomes less dense than air at the same level over the valley and flows up the slope. This is the anabatic wind: weak, about 5–10 kt, and often marked by Cu over the ridges. At night the slope cools by radiation, the air touching it becomes denser and drains down the slope under gravity: the katabatic wind. Katabatic winds can be strong where a large cold plateau or ice sheet feeds them, as in Greenland and Antarctica, and the Bora is partly katabatic. Katabatic flow fills valleys with cold air, giving valley fog, frost, an inversion and wind shear at the valley rim. Remember ana = up. 02.04.01.01

The same effect on the scale of a whole valley gives the valley wind, blowing up the valley towards the mountains by day, and the mountain wind, blowing down the valley at night. Both are strongest in summer, under clear skies and with a weak pressure gradient. At a valley aerodrome the runway in use may change between morning and afternoon. 02.04.01.02

2.10 Venturi effect

Air forced through a gap or a narrowing valley must speed up to get through (continuity), and as it speeds up its static pressure falls (Bernoulli). The Mistral down the Rhône valley, the Tramontane, and the Levante through the Strait of Gibraltar are examples. Expect much stronger local wind and turbulence in passes than the pressure gradient suggests, and remember from Chapter 1 that the altimeter over-reads in this low-pressure, accelerated flow. 02.04.01.03

2.11 Sea and land breezes

By day the land heats faster than the sea. Air rises over the land, a shallow thermal low forms at the surface, and air flows onshore at low level, with a return flow offshore aloft. This sea breeze is typically 10–15 kt and 1000–3000 ft deep, and pushes 10–30 nm inland, more in the tropics. It starts in mid-morning, peaks in mid-afternoon and, in the northern hemisphere, veers through the day as the Coriolis force acts on it. At night the land cools faster and a weaker land breeze of about 5 kt blows offshore. Both need strong heating and a weak synoptic pressure gradient, which is why they are common under a high. 02.04.01.04

The leading edge of the cool marine air is the sea-breeze front, a convergence line that can produce a line of Cu, sometimes showers or thunderstorms, wind shear and turbulence, and a drop in visibility from haze or smoke. At a coastal aerodrome the runway wind can reverse in the late morning, and sea fog can be carried inland.

2.12 The evening low-level jet

After sunset a surface radiation inversion separates the air above from the friction of the ground. Freed from friction, the wind just above the inversion accelerates and can become super-geostrophic, through an effect called inertial oscillation. It peaks around midnight to early morning, a few hundred to about 2000 ft above the ground. For a night or early-morning approach with a calm surface wind, expect strong shear between about 300 and 1500 ft and be ready for airspeed fluctuations. 02.04.01.05

2.13 Mountain waves

When stable air is forced up over a ridge, it is lifted away from the level where it would naturally rest. On the lee side it sinks back past that level, becomes warmer than its surroundings, bounces back up, and keeps oscillating as it travels downstream. The wind holds this oscillation in place relative to the ground, so the waves stand still: standing waves, or lee waves. Their energy can also travel upward to great heights. In unstable air the same lifting produces convection instead. 02.05.01.01

Mountain waves need three conditions:

  1. A wind blowing within about 30° of perpendicular to the ridge.
  2. A wind at ridge-top level of at least about 15 kt for small ridges, or 25 kt for large ranges, increasing with height with little change of direction.
  3. A stable layer near ridge-top level, with less stable air above and below it.

02.05.01.02

Exam trap. Distractors offer "unstable air at ridge level" or "wind decreasing with height". Both are wrong.

The waves typically have a wavelength of 2–30 km, longer with stronger wind and weaker stability. Their amplitude can reach several thousand feet, and vertical speeds can exceed 2000 ft/min. The strongest downdraft is on the immediate lee slope. Beneath the wave crests, at or below ridge-top height, rotors form: rolling eddies with severe turbulence. Above the rotor the flow in the wave itself is smooth and laminar, but an aircraft holding a constant attitude can still gain or lose several thousand feet. The waves can extend into the stratosphere. The most severe turbulence is in the rotor, below the crests, on the lee side, roughly at ridge height. 02.05.01.03

Mountain waves show themselves through cloud, when there is moisture:

  • Lenticular clouds (ACSL, CCSL, SCSL) are smooth, lens-shaped and stationary. They sit at the wave crests, sometimes stacked like a pile of plates. They do not drift with the wind: air flows through them, condensing on the way up and evaporating on the way down.
  • Rotor (roll) clouds are ragged lines of Cu or Sc parallel to the ridge, at low level under the crests.
  • A cap cloud, or Föhn wall, drapes over the ridge on the windward side, with a clear Föhn gap in the lee.

Without moisture the waves are invisible, so a clear sky does not mean there are no waves. 02.05.01.04

Mountain-wave downdrafts of 2000 ft/min or more can exceed the climb performance of light aircraft, and of heavy aircraft at high altitude; rotor turbulence can exceed structural limits; and the altimeter over-reads in the accelerated, low-pressure flow, which adds to the danger near terrain. In strong winds, cross ridges with a margin of at least half the ridge height and at about 45°, so that you can turn away; fly at turbulence penetration speed; and avoid the lee side at low level. 02.05.01.05

With favourable profiles of wind and stability, wave energy climbs to the tropopause and into the stratosphere, where the waves can break and produce clear-air turbulence at cruise levels. Well-known areas are Greenland, the Rockies, the Andes, the Alps, the Himalaya and Norway; on North Atlantic tracks, turbulence over Greenland at FL 300 and above is often mountain-wave turbulence. SWC charts mark areas of severe mountain wave (SEV MTW), and a SIGMET is issued for it. 02.05.01.06

2.14 Turbulence

Turbulence is irregular, random eddying motion of the air in all directions, which makes an aircraft's attitude, altitude and airspeed change rapidly and varies its load factor. Gustiness is the rapid fluctuation of the surface wind's speed and direction about its mean, caused by the same eddies; it is reported as a gust (G) when the peak exceeds the mean by 10 kt or more. On a gusty day, add the gust factor to the approach speed as your procedures require. The ICAO intensity scale (light, moderate, severe) is in Chapter 9. 02.06.01.01

There are five meteorological types of turbulence: convective (thermal), mechanical (friction with the ground and obstacles), orographic (mountains, waves and rotors), frontal (shear and lifting at fronts) and clear-air turbulence (high-level shear). Wake turbulence is aircraft-made, not meteorological. Each type has its forecast: convective turbulence goes with CB areas on the SWC chart, CAT with the CAT areas, and orographic turbulence with mountain-wave markings. 02.06.01.02

Each type forms in its own way:

  • Convective turbulence comes from uneven heating: thermals rise and compensating downdrafts sink. It is strongest on sunny afternoons over land, in and below Cu and Cb, so expect a bumpy approach below Cu bases on a summer afternoon. Above the cloud tops or an inversion the air is smoother.
  • Mechanical turbulence comes from wind blowing over rough ground, trees and buildings. It grows with wind speed, roughness and instability and stays within the friction layer. Expect it downwind of hangars and buildings on short final.
  • Orographic turbulence comes from air flowing over and around mountains: lee eddies, waves and rotors.
  • Frontal turbulence comes from the vertical shear and lifting across a frontal surface, and is strongest with fast-moving, active cold fronts and squall lines.

02.06.02.01

Turbulence is normally found near rough ground and relief (in the friction layer and the lee of hills); at inversions, where air layers slide over each other; in and near Cb and thunderstorms, up to 20 nm away and above their tops; in unstable layers; and near jet streams and tropopause breaks. Avoid Cb by at least 10 nm, or 20 nm when severe or at high level, and never fly under the anvil. Expect shear when crossing a low inversion on climb or descent, especially at night. 02.06.02.02

2.15 Clear-air turbulence

Clear-air turbulence (CAT) is turbulence at high level, usually above FL 200, in cloud-free air and not linked to convection. It is caused by strong wind shear. It is patchy, typically 50–100 nm long, 10–20 nm wide and 2000–5000 ft deep, and often lies in bands parallel to a jet stream. There is no visual warning and no radar return, which is why seat belts stay fastened while seated. 02.06.03.01

CAT forms where strong vertical (and horizontal) wind shear acts across a stable layer. Waves form on the boundary between the layers, grow and break into turbulent eddies, a process called Kelvin–Helmholtz instability. Turbulence appears when the shear is strong enough to overcome the stability, which is the idea behind the Richardson number. As a rule of thumb, forecasters expect CAT where the vertical shear reaches 5 kt per 1000 ft or the horizontal shear 20 kt per 100 nm, and severe CAT is likely above about 6 kt per 1000 ft. Shear comes from horizontal temperature gradients (the thermal wind, section 2.16), so tightly packed isotherms on a chart flag CAT. 02.06.03.02

CAT is found:

  • near jet streams, mainly on the cold (polar, low-pressure) side just below the core, and above the core near the tropopause break;
  • in sharply curved upper troughs and ridges, and wherever the jet curves;
  • at jet entrance and exit regions, and where streams of air converge or spread apart;
  • near tropopause breaks and in breaking mountain waves.

02.06.03.03

Exam trap. CAT is usually worst on the cold (low-pressure) side of the jet, not the warm side.

Clear air has no moisture or particles, so CAT cannot be seen by satellites or weather radar. Forecasts use indices of shear and deformation computed from numerical models (such as the Ellrod index), and they are probabilistic: a forecast CAT area means turbulence is possible there, and it can still occur outside. 02.06.03.04

Since nothing can measure CAT remotely, pilot reports (special air-reports, and automated reports of eddy dissipation rate) are the only direct observations. They feed SIGMETs and warn other crews, so report moderate or severe turbulence promptly, with position, flight level, time and aircraft type. 02.06.03.05

2.16 Jet streams

A jet stream is a strong, narrow, nearly horizontal current of air with its axis near the tropopause, with strong vertical and lateral wind shear and one or more speed maxima. Jets are a product of the thermal wind: where there is a strong horizontal temperature contrast, pressure surfaces slope more and more steeply with height (because cold columns are thinner than warm ones), so the geostrophic wind increases with height through that layer. In the northern hemisphere the thermal wind blows with cold air on its left, so the jets are mostly westerly. A jet can give a tailwind or headwind of 100–200 kt, and brings CAT with it; flight planning uses jets eastbound and avoids them westbound. 02.07.01.01

By the WMO definition a jet stream has a core speed of at least 60 kt. SWC charts only draw jets of 80 kt or more, as arrows with wind barbs and the flight level of the core, and in some formats with the vertical extent of the 80 kt isotach. 02.07.01.02

Exam trap. The definition is 60 kt. The SWC chart threshold is 80 kt. Distractors offer 50, 80 or 100 kt for the definition.

Jets are thousands of nautical miles long (in segments of often 1000–3000 nm), about 100–300 nm (200–500 km) wide and about 10 000–15 000 ft (3–5 km) deep. Core speeds are typically 100–200 kt and reach 250–300 kt over Japan in winter. Typical shear is 5–10 kt per 1000 ft vertically and 20–50 kt per 100 nm horizontally on the cold side. Because a jet is far wider than it is deep, changing level can take you out of the core faster than a sideways diversion. 02.07.01.03

There are four named jets:

Key numbers · jet streams

Jet Level Latitude Season and character
Arctic (front) ≈ FL 200–250 ≈ 60–70° Mainly winter, along the arctic front
Polar front ≈ FL 300–350 ≈ 40–65° Follows the polar front; further south and stronger in winter (≈ 40°, 150+ kt), further north and weaker in summer; variable, meanders with the long waves
Subtropical ≈ FL 400 (≈ 200 hPa) ≈ 25–30° in winter, ≈ 40° in summer Persistent, at the poleward edge of the Hadley cell; strongest in winter, maximum over Japan
Tropical easterly ≈ FL 450–500 (≈ 100–150 hPa) ≈ 10–20° N Northern summer only (June–September), over southern India, the Arabian Sea and Africa; easterly, ≈ 50–100 kt; linked to the SW monsoon

02.07.02.01

The subtropical jet is higher and more persistent; the polar front jet is more variable and goes with fronts and CAT.

Exam trap. The tropical jet is easterly, and it exists only in the northern summer.

2.17 Where the jet sits, and where the CAT is

The polar front jet lies in the warm air, just below the higher, warm-side tropopause, at the tropopause break. Because the frontal surface slopes upward towards the cold side, the jet core lies roughly 300–600 km poleward of the surface front, above air that is cold at the surface. Its maximum wind is below the tropopause, near FL 300–350. The arctic jet lies the same way relative to the arctic front, at a lower level. On satellite images the jet axis often runs along the sharp poleward edge of the frontal cirrus shield. 02.07.03.01

Exam trap. The jet core is not above the surface front, and not in the cold air. It is in the warm air, displaced poleward of the surface front.

The worst CAT and shear lie on the cold (polar, low-pressure) side of the jet just below the core, and in the stable layer above the core near the tropopause break; also where the jet curves sharply round upper troughs, and at jet exits. The greatest vertical shear is above and below the core; the greatest horizontal shear is on the cold side. To escape jet CAT, change level (often descending on the cold side or climbing above the core) or move sideways towards the warm side. A rapid change of outside air temperature at constant level suggests you are crossing the frontal zone near the jet: expect CAT. 02.07.03.02

Check yourself

  1. Why is the gradient wind round a low weaker than the geostrophic wind for the same isobar spacing? Round a low the pressure gradient force must supply the centripetal force as well as balance the Coriolis force, so the Coriolis force, and with it the wind speed, is smaller than geostrophic.
  2. In the southern hemisphere, the wind at 2000 ft over land is 180/30. Roughly what is the surface wind? Veered by about 30° and halved: about 210/15.
  3. Isobars are equally spaced at 40° N and 60° N. Where is the geostrophic wind stronger? At 40° N, because Vg is proportional to 1/sin φ.
  4. Name the three conditions for mountain waves. Wind within about 30° of perpendicular to the ridge; wind of at least 15–25 kt at ridge level, increasing with height; a stable layer near ridge level with less stable air above and below.
  5. Where is the most severe turbulence in a mountain-wave system? In the rotor zone on the lee side, below the wave crests, roughly at ridge height.
  6. What is the minimum speed of a jet stream, and from what speed are jets drawn on SWC charts? 60 kt by definition; 80 kt on SWC charts.
  7. On which side of a northern-hemisphere westerly jet is CAT usually worst? On the cold, polar side (the left side looking downwind), just below the core.
  8. What makes a surface depression deepen? Upper-level divergence exceeding low-level convergence.
