chapters.html:
Chapter 6 followed the frontal depression through its life. This chapter steps back to the other pressure systems: the great permanent and seasonal highs and lows, the different kinds of anticyclone and non-frontal low, and the most violent low of all, the tropical revolving storm.

7.1 The principal pressure areas

Some pressure systems are permanent features of the map. The subtropical highs sit over the oceans at about 30°: the Azores (or Bermuda) high, the North Pacific (Hawaiian) high, and in the southern hemisphere the South Atlantic (St Helena), South Indian (Mascarene) and South Pacific highs. The subpolar lows, the Icelandic and Aleutian lows, are deepest in winter. The Icelandic low is not a single stationary low but the statistical average of the depressions that keep passing through. Near the equator lies the equatorial trough. 07.01.01.01

Other systems come and go with the seasons, as the continents heat and cool:

  • In January (northern winter) the Siberian high is the strongest pressure system on Earth, often above 1035 hPa, with the North American (Canadian) high alongside it. The Icelandic and Aleutian lows are deep, and thermal lows sit over southern Africa, Australia and South America, where it is summer.
  • In July (northern summer) a large thermal low covers South Asia (the Pakistan or Persian Gulf low), with smaller ones over the south-western USA, Iberia and the Sahara. The Azores and Pacific highs are strong and displaced north, the Icelandic low is weak, and a high covers Australia in its winter.

On a map, the Siberian high belongs only to winter and the Asian low only to summer.

The systems form in two different ways. Dynamic systems are made by the circulation: the subtropical highs by the sinking branch of the Hadley cell, where air converges aloft at about 30°, and the subpolar lows by convergence and ascent at the polar front and the constant passage of depressions. Thermal systems are made by the surface: continental winter highs by intense radiative cooling of dense air, so they are shallow and cold-cored; continental summer lows by strong surface heating, so they are shallow and warm-cored. The equatorial trough comes from heating and from the convergence of the trade winds. As Chapter 1 showed, thermal systems are shallow and reverse with height, while the dynamic subtropical highs are deep, warm highs. 07.01.01.02

The whole pattern follows the sun, moving poleward in the summer hemisphere and equatorward in winter, about one to two months behind the sun. It moves further over the continents than over the oceans, and the continental thermal highs and lows reverse between the seasons. Spain shows this clearly: in summer it lies under the Azores ridge with a thermal low over the Iberian interior, bringing heat and afternoon thunderstorms inland; in winter it lies in the path of Atlantic depressions, with occasional outbreaks of continental polar air. 07.01.01.03

7.2 Anticyclones

There are four kinds of anticyclone. Warm anticyclones are dynamic, deep and warm-cored, like the subtropical highs. Cold anticyclones are thermal, shallow and cold-cored, like the continental winter highs and polar highs. Ridges are wedges of high pressure between lows. Blocking highs are persistent warm highs at middle and high latitudes. Depth is what tells warm and cold highs apart: a warm high reaches the tropopause, a cold high disappears aloft. 07.02.01.01

A surface high forms where air converges aloft: behind upper troughs, at certain quadrants of jet streams, and in the descending branch of the Hadley cell. Air accumulates in the column, and if the upper convergence exceeds the divergence at the surface, the surface pressure rises. The extra air sinks and spreads out at the surface. A surface high therefore means divergence at low level, subsidence through the column and convergence aloft. 07.02.01.02

Subsiding air warms at the DALR and dries. The top of a subsiding layer sinks further than its bottom, so it warms more, the lapse rate becomes stable, and a subsidence inversion forms, typically at 3000–6000 ft and lowering with time. Above it there is little cloud and light wind; beneath it haze, smoke and Sc collect, or fog and stratus in winter. Subsidence explains both the clear skies of highs and their persistent poor visibility and anticyclonic gloom. 07.02.01.03

A warm anticyclone is built dynamically, by convergence aloft and subsidence. Its column is warm, so it strengthens with height; subtropical and blocking highs are of this type. A cold anticyclone is built thermally, by intense radiative cooling of air over snow-covered continents in winter. Its column is cold and dense, so pressure is high at the surface but the system weakens with height and becomes a low aloft. The Siberian high is cold and shallow; the Azores high is warm and deep. 07.02.01.04

A ridge is an elongated extension of a high, typically lying between two depressions in the westerlies, in the cold air behind one and ahead of the next. It brings subsidence and surface divergence and moves along with the family of depressions. Its isobars are U-shaped around the axis, and in the northern hemisphere the wind backs as a ridge passes, after veering in the trough before it. 07.02.01.05

The two kinds of anticyclone bring different weather. A warm high gives fine, settled weather, light winds and little cloud, or Sc under the inversion. In summer that means heat, haze and possibly isolated thunderstorms at its edges; in winter over land, fog, stratus and anticyclonic gloom. A cold high gives very cold, dry air, clear skies, severe frost, radiation fog or ice fog, poor visibility in smoke haze, and low stratus under its inversion. In winter, fog and stratus at dawn under a high can close many aerodromes at once, while above the inversion flying conditions are good. 07.02.01.06

A ridge brings a fair-weather interval between fronts: subsidence clears the cloud, winds are light and visibility good in the fresh polar air, though radiation fog can form at night in winter. It is short-lived, and increasing cirrus on its western side announces the next front. Treat a ridge as a good VFR window, with the next frontal system due within 12–24 hours. 07.02.01.07

A blocking anticyclone is a persistent warm high at middle or high latitudes, over Scandinavia or the British Isles for example, that interrupts the westerly flow. Seen on the upper chart, the flow around it can take the shape of the Greek letter omega (an omega block). Depressions are deflected north and south of it and slow down. A block lasts from days to weeks. Under it the weather stays settled, with heatwaves in summer and cold spells, fog and smog in winter; at its flanks depressions stall and bring persistent rain; and unusual easterly winds blow over Europe. Atlantic tracks shift to route around it. 07.02.01.08

7.3 Non-frontal depressions

A surface low forms where air diverges aloft: ahead of upper troughs and at certain quadrants of jet streams. Air is removed from the column faster than low-level convergence replaces it, so the surface pressure falls and the low deepens, while air rises through the column making cloud and precipitation. Deepening lows are therefore found downstream of upper troughs, under upper divergence. 07.03.01.01

Four kinds of low form without fronts, or apart from them:

  • A thermal low forms over land heated strongly in summer, as over Iberia, the Sahara and northern India. It is shallow and warm-cored, with a weak circulation and a high above it, and brings afternoon thunderstorms if the air is moist enough.
  • An orographic or lee low forms when air flows across a mountain range: the air descending the lee side is stretched vertically and the pressure falls. The Genoa low south of the Alps in northerly flow, and lows in the lee of the Rockies, are examples. They can grow into active depressions with severe weather. Genoa lows bring severe weather to the western Mediterranean, Italy and the Alps, often with the Mistral or Bora (Chapter 8).
  • A polar low is a small (about 200–500 km), intense low that forms in very cold arctic air over a relatively warm sea in winter. It brings heavy snow showers, gales and Cb, forms and deepens quickly, and is hard to forecast.
  • A secondary low forms within the circulation of a main depression, often on its trailing cold front or at the triple point. It can deepen rapidly, take over from the primary, and bring worse weather than it.

07.03.01.02

A trough is an elongated area of low pressure, with V-shaped isobars, extending from a low. Air converges and rises along it. Frontal troughs contain fronts; non-frontal troughs, such as troughs in the polar air behind a cold front or troughs in the upper air, bring bands of showers and thunderstorms. In the northern hemisphere the wind veers as a trough passes, and pressure falls ahead of it and rises behind it. Behind a cold front, a non-frontal trough may bring a second line of showers, and upper troughs at 500 hPa drive surface development and convection. 07.03.01.03

7.4 Tropical revolving storms

A tropical revolving storm (TRS) needs five ingredients:

  1. A sea-surface temperature of at least 26–27 °C through a deep layer of about 50 m.
  2. A latitude of at least 5°, because the Coriolis force is needed to start the rotation. A TRS never forms on the equator.
  3. High humidity through the troposphere, in conditionally unstable air.
  4. Weak vertical wind shear; strong shear tears the warm core apart.
  5. A disturbance to start it, such as an easterly wave or a disturbance in the ITCZ, with divergence aloft.

Because of cold currents and shear, tropical revolving storms do not form in the South Atlantic or south-east Pacific, and none form within about 5° of the equator. Their energy comes from the latent heat of the warm sea, so they weaken quickly over land or cold water. 07.04.01.01

A TRS is steered by the flow around it. In the northern hemisphere it first moves west or west-north-west with the trade winds on the equatorward side of the subtropical high, at about 10–15 kt. It then recurves poleward and north-eastward around the western edge of the high into the westerlies, speeding up to 20–30 kt or more. In the southern hemisphere the track is a mirror image: west-south-west, then recurving to the south-east. After recurving the storm often becomes an extra-tropical low, which can still be dangerous at mid-latitudes. 07.04.01.02

The stages are defined by the maximum sustained wind:

Key numbers · stages of a tropical revolving storm

Stage Maximum sustained wind
Tropical disturbance Organised convection, no closed circulation
Tropical depression Closed circulation, under 34 kt
Tropical storm (named) 34–47 kt
Severe tropical storm 48–63 kt
Tropical revolving storm (hurricane, typhoon, cyclone) 64 kt or more (hurricane force, Beaufort 12)

07.04.01.03

Inside the storm:

  • The eye, about 10–40 nm across, has light winds, little cloud, subsiding warm air and the lowest pressure, which can fall below 920 hPa.
  • The eyewall, a ring of Cb reaching the tropopause around the eye, has the strongest winds (64 kt and up to more than 150 kt), torrential rain, and severe turbulence and icing.
  • Spiral rain bands of Cb and thunderstorms curl in towards the centre, with gusts and squalls.
  • Aloft, a cirrus shield spreads out from the anticyclonic outflow. At the coast, the storm surge brings flooding.

The strongest winds and worst weather are in the eyewall, often on the right-hand side of the track (poleward and forward) in the northern hemisphere. Aerodromes close, and aircraft must be flown out or secured. 07.04.01.04

The circulation of a TRS is about 200–500 nm across, with gale-force winds over about 100–300 nm, an eye of about 10–40 nm, and cloud reaching the tropopause at about FL 500 or higher. Avoid it by hundreds of miles, not tens. 07.04.01.05

A TRS's track can stall, loop or recurve unexpectedly, and its strength can grow very fast (rapid intensification). Its movement can only rarely be forecast exactly, and forecast cones widen with lead time, so take the utmost care near one: use the latest advisories from the Tropical Cyclone Advisory Centres and SIGMETs (Chapter 10), and carry generous fuel and alternates. 07.04.01.06

7.5 Where and when tropical revolving storms occur

The storms have different names in different oceans:

  • Hurricane in the North Atlantic, the Caribbean, the Gulf of Mexico and the north-east Pacific off Mexico.
  • Typhoon in the north-west Pacific (the Philippines, China and Japan).
  • Cyclone or tropical cyclone in the North Indian Ocean (the Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea), the South Indian Ocean (Madagascar and Mauritius), around Australia and in the south-west Pacific. Australia historically also used the name willy-willy.

There are none in the South Atlantic (with rare exceptions) or the south-east Pacific. 07.04.02.01

Key numbers · tropical revolving storm seasons

Area Season Frequency
North Atlantic June–November, peak August–October ≈ 10–15 named storms a year, ≈ 6 hurricanes
North-east Pacific May/June–November —
North-west Pacific All year, peak July–October Most frequent basin, ≈ 25–30 storms a year
North Indian Ocean April–June and October–December ≈ 5 a year
South Indian Ocean, Australia, south-west Pacific November–April, peak January–March —

The Bay of Bengal has two seasons, before and after the south-west monsoon, with little activity during the monsoon itself because of strong shear. 07.04.02.02

Check yourself

  1. Why does the Siberian high not appear on a 300 hPa chart? It is a cold, thermal high: its dense, cold column makes it shallow, and it becomes a low aloft.
  2. Where does a subsidence inversion form, and what weather does it bring? In an anticyclone, typically at 3000–6000 ft. Clear skies above; haze, smoke, Sc, or fog and stratus in winter, trapped beneath.
  3. What sets a blocking high apart from an ordinary ridge? It is a persistent warm high that interrupts the westerlies for days or weeks, deflecting depressions around it; a ridge is a transient wedge between two depressions.
  4. Why does a tropical revolving storm never form at the equator? The Coriolis force there is zero, so no rotation can develop. A latitude of at least 5° is needed.
  5. A tropical storm has maximum sustained winds of 55 kt. What stage is it? Severe tropical storm (48–63 kt).
  6. In which season do cyclones affect the Bay of Bengal? April–June and October–December, before and after the south-west monsoon.
  7. Where is a Genoa low, and what forms it? South of the Alps, in the lee of the mountains, when northerly flow crosses the Alps.

chapters.label: Chapter 8
chapters.title: Climatology
chapters.html:
Climatology is the weather you can expect at a place and season before you look at any forecast. It follows from the global circulation of Chapter 2 and its seasonal march with the sun. This chapter covers the climate zones, the tropics (trade winds, the ITCZ, monsoons, squall lines, easterly waves and sandstorms), the typical weather situations of the mid-latitudes, and the best-known local winds.

8.1 The general circulation again

The circulation of Chapter 2 sets the climate. At the surface there are the Hadley cells, with ascent in the ITCZ and subsidence in the subtropics; the mid-latitude westerlies, with travelling depressions along the polar front; and the polar easterlies. In the upper troposphere the flow is westerly, with the subtropical and polar front jets, and easterly over the tropics in summer. In the lower stratosphere the winds are westerly in winter, with the strong polar night jet at high levels, and easterly in summer. Climatology questions combine this pattern with its seasonal shift, so learn which belt controls a region in January and in July. 08.01.01.01

8.2 Climate zones

There are five main climates:

  • The tropical rain climate (A) is warm all year, with the coldest month above 18 °C, high humidity and heavy convective rain. It includes rainforest, and savanna and monsoon climates with distinct wet and dry seasons.
  • The dry climate (B) is where evaporation exceeds precipitation: deserts and steppes, with a large daily temperature range, dust and strong heating.
  • The mid-latitude, or warm temperate rain, climate (C) has mild winters (coldest month between −3 and 18 °C) and frontal precipitation. It includes the Mediterranean climate, with a dry summer, and the maritime west-coast climate.
  • The subarctic, or cold snow-forest, climate (D) has cold winters with snow cover (coldest month below −3 °C) and short, warm summers. It covers the continental interiors of North America and Eurasia (the taiga).
  • The snow, or polar, climate (E) has its warmest month below 10 °C. It includes tundra and ice caps.

Spain is mostly Mediterranean (C, dry summer), with semi-arid (B) areas in the south-east. 08.01.02.01

Because the pressure and wind belts follow the sun, some regions lie in one belt in summer and another in winter, and these form transitional climates. The savanna gets ITCZ rains in summer and dry trade winds in winter. The Mediterranean lies under the subtropical high in summer, which makes it dry, and in the westerlies in winter, when polar-front depressions bring rain. Monsoon regions see their wind reverse. 08.01.02.02

Key numbers · where the climate zones lie

Climate Latitude Examples
Tropical rain ≈ 0–15° (savanna and monsoon to ≈ 20°) Amazon, Congo, Indonesia
Dry ≈ 15–35°, western sides of continents and interiors Sahara, Arabia, Kalahari, Atacama, central Australia, south-west USA
Mid-latitude ≈ 35–55° Western Europe, the Mediterranean, eastern USA, eastern China
Subarctic ≈ 50–70°, continental interiors Siberia, Canada
Polar Above ≈ 65–70° Greenland, Antarctica

Deserts lie under the subtropical highs, on the side of each continent where cold ocean currents run. 08.01.02.03

8.3 Tropical showers and thunderstorms

Tropical showers and thunderstorms need very warm, humid air at the surface, deep conditional instability, a high tropopause (so Cb tops reach FL 500–600), and something to lift the air: convergence (the ITCZ, easterly waves, sea-breeze fronts), mountains or daytime heating. The convection organises into cloud clusters hundreds of kilometres across and into mesoscale convective complexes (MCCs): long-lived (more than 6 hours), large (a cold cloud shield of over 100 000 km²) and often at their most active at night. Over land the maximum is in the afternoon and evening, over the sea at night and early morning. Cb embedded in huge cloud shields make weather radar essential, and bring a risk of ice-crystal icing (Chapter 9). 08.02.01.01

A tropical squall line is an organised line of Cb several hundred kilometres long, moving faster than the mean wind (in West Africa often westward at about 20–30 kt). It arrives with a gust front: a sharp wind shift, gusts of 40–60 kt or more and a sudden drop in temperature, then heavy rain for about an hour, followed by lighter rain from stratiform cloud behind. The "line squalls" of the West African wet season are the classic example. They bring severe turbulence, wind shear, heavy rain and low visibility at aerodromes, cannot be overflown, and are not easy to fly around. 08.02.01.02

The Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) is where the north-east and south-east trade winds meet. The converging moist, unstable air is forced to rise, building bands and clusters of Cu and Cb rather than a continuous wall. Activity is strongest over land in summer and where the convergence is strongest, and weak or broken over some oceans. The ITCZ is not a front: there is no temperature contrast across it, only convergence. 08.02.01.03

In the tropics the surface temperature is typically 25–30 °C (higher inland in the dry season), the dew point 20–25 °C and the relative humidity often above 70–80 %. The freezing level stays at about 15 000–16 000 ft (FL 150–160) all year. Airframe icing is therefore confined to higher levels, though tropical Cb carry supercooled water and ice crystals far above that. The hot, humid surface air also means a high density altitude. 08.02.01.04

8.4 Tropical winds and pressure belts

The trade winds are the tropical easterlies, blowing steadily from the north-east in the northern hemisphere and the south-east in the southern, from the subtropical highs towards the ITCZ, at about 10–20 kt. A trade-wind inversion, formed by subsidence at about 5000–8000 ft, caps the convection. Under it lie fair-weather Cu with flat tops and good visibility, and showers fall mainly on the windward slopes of islands. The inversion rises and weakens towards the ITCZ. Below about FL 100 the trades usually give good flying weather, except near windward mountains. 08.02.02.01

The doldrums are the equatorial belt of low pressure, mainly over the oceans, within the ITCZ zone. Winds are light and variable, or calm; the air is hot and humid; and Cb with heavy showers and thunderstorms develop, especially in the afternoon and at night. They bring all the hazards of the ITCZ. 08.02.02.02

The subtropical highs, at about 25–35° (the horse latitudes), lie under the sinking branch of the Hadley cell. Subsidence gives light, variable winds and clear skies, or low Sc under the inversion over the eastern oceans; the air is dry, deserts lie beneath on land, and there is haze and dust. Along coasts with cold currents under these highs (California, Morocco, Namibia, Peru), fog and stratus are common. 08.02.02.03

The major monsoons are:

  • South Asia: the south-west monsoon in June–September (wet) and the north-east monsoon in December–February (dry).
  • West Africa: the south-west monsoon in summer (wet) and the north-east trade, the Harmattan, in winter (dry and dusty).
  • East Asia: the south or south-east summer monsoon (wet) and the north or north-west winter monsoon (cold and dry, from the Siberian high).
  • Northern Australia: the north-west monsoon in December–March (wet) and the south-east trades in winter (dry).

On a July map, the south-west monsoon over India is the one to identify. 08.02.02.04

8.5 The ITCZ through the year

Key numbers · ITCZ positions

Region January July
West Africa Near the Guinea coast (≈ 5° N) ≈ 15–20° N
India and Pakistan South of the equator Up to ≈ 25–30° N (monsoon trough)
Southern Africa, northern Australia, Brazil ≈ 10–20° S North of the equator
Eastern Atlantic and eastern Pacific ≈ 0–5° N (stays north of the equator) ≈ 5–10° N

08.02.03.01

Over the eastern Atlantic and eastern Pacific the ITCZ stays in the northern hemisphere all year, and its seasonal swing is largest over Africa and Asia. It follows the zone of greatest heating, under the overhead sun, about one to two months behind it, and moves much further over the continents, with their low heat capacity, than over the oceans. Its position decides the wet and dry seasons in the tropics. In West Africa, for example, the ITCZ lies north in July, bringing the wet season and line squalls, and south in January, bringing the Harmattan. 08.02.03.02

At the ITCZ the winds are light and variable where the trades meet. Cu and Cb form lines and clusters, with heavy showers and thunderstorms and tops at FL 450–600. Activity varies along its length, peaking over land in the afternoon and evening and over the sea at night. Its width varies from a narrow line to a broad zone hundreds of kilometres wide. Because it is not continuous, crews choose a crossing point with less activity using satellite pictures and radar. 08.02.03.03

The ITCZ's flight hazards are severe turbulence in Cb; icing above the freezing level (about FL 150), including high concentrations of ice crystals (ice-crystal icing) in and near Cb anvils; hail; lightning; heavy rain, with engine water ingestion and poor visibility; wind shear; and sand and dust in squalls over Africa. Signs of ice-crystal icing include rain on the windscreen at sub-zero temperatures, odd total air temperature readings, and only light radar returns in heavy cloud. 08.02.03.04

8.6 Monsoons

A monsoon is a seasonal reversal of the prevailing wind, by at least 120°, caused by the different heating of continents and oceans, and bringing wet and dry seasons with it. The main regions are South and South-East Asia, East Asia, West Africa and northern Australia. "Monsoon" means the wind regime, not just the rain. 08.02.04.01

Monsoon winds are trade winds that have crossed the equator. When the ITCZ moves far into the summer hemisphere, the trades of the winter hemisphere follow it across the equator. There the Coriolis force changes direction, so the south-east trades are turned to the right and become the south-west monsoon of India and West Africa, and the north-east trades crossing into the southern hemisphere become the north-west monsoon of northern Australia. The long sea track makes them very moist and unstable. That is why the Indian summer monsoon is south-westerly. 08.02.04.03

The wet (summer) monsoon brings deep, moist, unstable air: extensive Cu, Cb and Ns; heavy, prolonged rain and thunderstorms; low ceilings and visibility; embedded Cb; and flooding. Its onset is often violent. The dry (winter) monsoon is a dry offshore flow, with fair weather, haze, dust and, in some areas such as northern India, fog. In the wet monsoon expect contaminated runways, wind shear, engine water ingestion in heavy rain and poor visibility; in the dry monsoon, haze and fog (the winter fog of Delhi, for example). 08.02.04.04

Over West Africa, from about June to September the ITCZ lies at about 15–20° N and a moist south-west monsoon flows in from the Gulf of Guinea. This is the rainy season, with westward-moving line squalls and thunderstorms; south of the ITCZ there is low cloud and drizzle near the coast. From about November to March the ITCZ lies near the Guinea coast and the dry north-east Harmattan blows from the Sahara, bringing dust haze, visibility often below 1000 m and little cloud. The hazard is visibility in winter and convection in summer. 08.02.04.05

Over India, the south-west monsoon (June–September) is drawn in by the Asian thermal low and the northward ITCZ, bringing moist air from the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal. It reaches Kerala in early June and covers India by mid-July, with heavy rain on the west coast (the Western Ghats) and in the north-east, Cb, thunderstorms and monsoon depressions; cyclones form in the Bay of Bengal before and after it. The north-east monsoon (December–February) is a dry outflow from the Siberian high, with fair weather and fog and haze in the north (the Ganges plain); only south-east India and Sri Lanka get rain, from the flow crossing the Bay of Bengal. Delhi therefore sees thunderstorms in the south-west monsoon, dust storms just before it, and dense fog in winter. 08.02.04.06

Over the Far East, the summer monsoon blows from the south or south-east and is wet, with the Baiu or Meiyu frontal rains over China and Japan in June and July, and typhoons from July to October. The winter monsoon blows cold and dry from the north or north-west out of the Siberian high; after crossing the Sea of Japan it brings snow to Japan's west coast. The strong winter contrast between continent and ocean is also why the strongest jet streams lie over Japan in winter. Over northern Australia the north-west monsoon of December to March is the wet season, with thunderstorms and cyclones, and the south-east trades of April to October bring the dry season. 08.02.04.07

8.7 Sandstorms and cold outbreaks

A sandstorm or dust storm happens when strong surface winds, above about 15–20 kt, blow over dry, loose sand or dust in unstable, well-mixed air. The wind may come from a Cb outflow (the gust front of a haboob), a cold front, a strong pressure gradient, or a local wind such as the Harmattan, Khamsin, Shamal or Ghibli. Dust can rise to FL 100–150 and travel thousands of kilometres. METARs report DS (dust storm), SS (sandstorm), BLSA or BLDU (blowing sand or dust), and +DS or +SS when visibility is below 200 m. The hazards are visibility below 1000 m, abrasion, engine erosion, blocked pitot and static ports, and walls of dust arriving without the warning of lightning. 08.02.04.08

In winter, cold polar air can surge a long way towards the equator behind strong cold fronts, especially along the eastern sides of continents and across open plains. Such outbreaks reach the Gulf of Mexico and Central America (the "northers"), the South American pampas, the South China Sea and northern India. They bring sharp falls in temperature, strong winds and sometimes snow at low latitudes, with gusty winds, low-level turbulence, icing and snow where pilots do not normally expect them. 08.02.04.09

Two outbreaks have names. The blizzard is a North American winter storm behind a deep low or cold front, with strong winds (30–35 kt or more), heavy falling or blowing snow, visibility of 400 m or less, and severe cold. The pampero is a cold, strong south-westerly wind over the pampas of Argentina and Uruguay behind a cold front, often arriving as a squall line with thunderstorms and a sharp drop in temperature. Pampero is South America; blizzard is North America. 08.02.04.10

8.8 Easterly waves

Easterly waves are wave-shaped troughs in the trade-wind easterlies. They move westward at about 10–15 kt, with a wavelength of about 2000–4000 km and a period of 3–4 days. Ahead of the trough axis (to its west) the air diverges and the weather is fair. Behind it (to its east) the air converges, the trade inversion lifts, and deep Cb, showers and thunderstorms develop. Many North Atlantic hurricanes grow from easterly waves that leave Africa. Note that the worst weather lies behind the axis, the opposite of what you would expect from a mid-latitude trough. 08.02.05.01

8.9 Typical mid-latitude situations

In a westerly situation a strong west-to-east flow crosses the mid-latitudes, and a family of frontal depressions forms on the polar front and runs quickly east at about 25–40 kt, separated by short-lived ridges. The surface chart shows closely spaced isobars running roughly west to east, with several lows in a row from the Atlantic to Scandinavia. The weather changes every day or two (frontal rain, then showers, then a brief ridge), winds are strong, and eastbound flights get good tailwinds. 08.03.01.01

High-pressure situations include the Azores high extending ridges over Europe, continental winter highs, and blocking highs. All bring subsidence, light winds and dry air: in summer, sun, heat, haze and isolated thunderstorms at the edges; in winter, fog, low stratus, frost and inversions trapping pollution (Chapter 7 describes warm and cold highs in detail). 08.03.02.01

On a chart, a high appears as closed isobars with pressure rising towards the centre (marked H), widely spaced isobars, U-shaped ridges extending from it, clockwise circulation in the northern hemisphere, and usually no fronts near its centre. Combine the chart with station reports: a small temperature–dew point spread and calm wind under a winter high mean a fog forecast. 08.03.02.02

8.10 The cold-air drop

A cold-air drop, also called a cold pool or cut-off low (in Spain, a DANA, depresión aislada en niveles altos), is an isolated pool of cold air in the middle and upper troposphere, with a closed cyclonic circulation aloft, cut off from the main westerly flow. It often has little or no sign on the surface chart. 08.03.04.01

It forms when an upper trough in a strongly meandering westerly flow deepens and stretches towards the equator, and its southern end is cut off as the flow to the north reconnects. The cold-cored low then drifts slowly and erratically, often for several days, sometimes even westward, until it is reabsorbed or fills. Its movement is slow and hard to forecast. 08.03.04.02

On upper-air charts (500 or 300 hPa) a cold-air drop shows as closed low contours with a cold centre (closed isotherms), separated from the westerly belt. On the surface chart it may show only as a weak low, a trough, or even slack or high pressure. On satellite images it appears as a comma or spiral of convective cloud. Always check the upper charts, because the surface chart alone can look harmless. 08.03.04.03

Cold air aloft over a warm surface, especially a warm sea such as the Mediterranean in autumn, makes the atmosphere strongly unstable. The result is severe Cb, hail, heavy and persistent rain (the autumn flash floods of Spain's Mediterranean coast), icing and turbulence, in an area of bad weather that moves slowly and unpredictably. Forecasts are unreliable, and severe weather can occur with no front at all, so carry extra fuel and choose alternates outside the area. 08.03.04.04

8.11 Local winds

The Föhn mechanism was worked through in Chapter 3. Moist air climbs the windward side, cooling at the DALR and then at the SALR in cloud while precipitation falls, and descends the lee side dry at the DALR, arriving warmer and drier than at the same level to windward. A second mechanism contributes: when the low-level air on the windward side is blocked by the mountains, the air descending in the lee comes from higher up, where it was potentially warmer. The Chinook is the Föhn east of the Rocky Mountains; the Zonda (Andes) and the berg wind (South Africa) are others. A Chinook can raise the temperature by 20 °C in a few hours and melt snow rapidly, earning its name "snow eater". 08.04.01.01

On the windward side of a Föhn there is extensive cloud and precipitation and the mountains are hidden behind the Föhn wall. In the lee the wind is warm, dry and gusty, the humidity low and the visibility excellent, with a clear Föhn gap in the cloud and lenticular clouds above. Lee aerodromes get strong, gusty crosswinds, wind shear and severe turbulence from mountain waves and rotors, despite clear skies. 08.04.01.02

The Mistral is a cold, dry, strong north or north-west wind that blows down the Rhône valley into the Gulf of Lion. It is funnelled between the Alps and the Massif Central (a Venturi effect) and is partly katabatic. It blows when cold air pours in behind a cold front, with high pressure over France or Biscay and low pressure over the Gulf of Genoa. Speeds are often 30–50 kt with gusts of 60–80 kt or more; skies are clear, visibility excellent, and it extends well out to sea. The Tramontane of Languedoc and Catalonia is a related wind. The Bora is a cold, dry, very gusty north-east katabatic wind that falls from the Dinaric Alps onto the Adriatic coast (Trieste and Croatia), when cold air pools over the Balkan plateau with low pressure over the Adriatic. Its gusts can exceed 100 kt, and the sky is often cloudless or has a cap cloud over the mountains. Both bring severe low-level turbulence, strong crosswinds and wind shear, and ice ships with sea spray; Marseille, Montpellier, Split and Trieste are among the aerodromes affected. Mistral is the Rhône and France; Bora is the Adriatic and Croatia. 08.04.01.03

The Harmattan is the dry, dusty north-east trade wind that blows from the Sahara over West Africa in the dry season, about November to March, when the ITCZ lies near the Gulf of Guinea. It carries fine dust, sometimes up to FL 100–150, making an extensive haze that can last for days. Visibility is often 1000–3000 m and at times below 1000 m over large areas, slant visibility on approach is very poor, and the METAR shows HZ or DU. There is little cloud: the hazard is visibility, not convection. 08.04.02.01

Check yourself

  1. Why is the Indian summer monsoon south-westerly when it starts as the south-east trade? Crossing the equator, the air comes under a Coriolis force acting to the right instead of the left, so it turns from south-east to south-west.
  2. Where is the ITCZ over West Africa in July, and what weather does it bring? At about 15–20° N: the wet season, with line squalls and thunderstorms.
  3. What is the freezing level in the tropics? About 15 000–16 000 ft all year.
  4. On which side of an easterly wave's axis is the weather worst? Behind it, to the east, where the air converges.
  5. Why can a cold-air drop be missed on a surface chart? It is a cold low in the middle and upper troposphere; at the surface it may show only as a weak low, a trough, or even high pressure.
  6. Mistral or Bora: which blows onto the Adriatic coast? The Bora.
  7. What is the main aviation hazard of the Harmattan? Poor visibility in dust haze, often below 1000 m, especially slant visibility on approach.

sections.title: 9.1 When ice forms on an aircraft
9.3 Icing hazards and how to avoid them

chapters.html:
Everything in the earlier chapters comes together here, as the weather that can damage or bring down an aircraft: icing, turbulence, wind shear, thunderstorms, tornadoes, inversions, the stratosphere, mountains and poor visibility. For each hazard the chapter explains the cause, how to recognise it and how to avoid it, and gives the ICAO terms used to report it.

9.1 When ice forms on an aircraft

Ice builds up on an aircraft when two things are true: its surface is at or below 0 °C, and there is supercooled liquid water (in cloud, fog, drizzle or rain) or water vapour that can deposit directly as ice (hoar frost). In practice airframe icing happens between 0 and −40 °C, and is most frequent and most severe between 0 and −15 °C. The airframe is not always at air temperature: after a long cold cruise it can be colder (cold soak), and at high speed it is warmer (kinetic heating). With the outside air slightly above 0 °C, ice can still form on a cold-soaked surface or on a probe cooled by expansion, which is why manuals call for anti-ice whenever there is visible moisture and a temperature at or below about +10 °C (typically for jets, using TAT) or +5 °C. 09.01.01.01

A venturi carburettor cools the air passing through it in two ways: the pressure drop in the venturi cools it adiabatically, and evaporating fuel takes latent heat. Together they can cool the intake air by 20–30 °C. If the air is humid, its vapour condenses and freezes in the venturi and on the throttle valve. Carburettor icing is possible at outside air temperatures from about −10 °C to +30 °C, and most likely with high humidity (a small spread) and temperatures between about 0 and +20 °C. It is worst at low power, with the throttle partly closed, as in a descent, and it can happen in clear air. Use carburettor heat as the aircraft's manual says: expect the RPM to drop at first, then rise as the ice melts. 09.01.01.02

Exam trap. Carburettor icing does not need sub-zero air. It is most common well above 0 °C.

Airframe ice forms in cloud or precipitation that contains supercooled water: Cu, Cb, Ns, Sc, St and As below 0 °C; freezing rain or drizzle beneath a warm-front inversion; and freezing fog. Icing becomes more severe with more liquid water, larger drops and temperatures nearer 0 to −10 °C. The worst situations are Cb, freezing rain under warm fronts, supercooled large drops in St and Sc, and cloud forced up over mountains. 09.01.01.03

As Chapter 3 explained, droplets cooled below 0 °C stay liquid because freezing nuclei are scarce. In cloud, rising air cools the droplets below zero; in freezing rain, rain from a warm layer falls into sub-zero air and supercools; and freezing drizzle often forms within supercooled St or Sc by coalescence. Supercooled large drops (SLD) can lie outside the conditions an aircraft was certified for: CS-25 Appendix C covers ordinary icing, and the separate Appendix O covers SLD. 09.01.01.04

The colder the air, the less supercooled water it holds: it can carry less vapour, and more freezing nuclei become active. The amount is greatest from 0 to −10 °C, moderate down to −20 °C, small below −20 °C (except in strong Cb updrafts) and practically nil below −40 °C. To escape icing, climb to colder air below −20 °C or descend into air above freezing. 09.01.01.05

Cloud type changes the droplets. Cumuliform cloud, with strong updrafts, holds large droplets and a high liquid water content (up to several grams per cubic metre), so ice builds fast, but only over short distances: intense, brief, clear icing. Stratiform cloud, with weak updrafts, holds small droplets and less water (about 0.1–0.5 g/m³), but over large distances: lighter, prolonged rime. 09.01.01.06

On the ground, ice can form whenever the surface is at or below 0 °C, and even with the outside air at +3 to +5 °C if the wings are cold-soaked. It comes from frost (after a clear night, when the surface falls below the frost point), freezing fog, snow, sleet, freezing drizzle or rain, rain or high humidity on cold-soaked surfaces, and snow or slush thrown up while taxiing. The clean aircraft rule applies: no take-off with frost, ice or snow on critical surfaces, which means de-icing, anti-icing and respecting holdover times. 09.01.01.07

In flight, ice forms inside cloud from supercooled droplets, and in precipitation from freezing rain or drizzle (even below the cloud) and wet snow. It can also form outside cloud and precipitation: hoar frost forms when an aircraft cold-soaked at altitude descends into warm, moist air, or flies from a cold layer into a warm, humid one. Clear air is no guarantee of no ice. 09.01.01.08

After a long flight at cold altitude, the fuel in the wing tanks can stay at −20 °C or colder. On the ground, the wing skin over the tanks stays below zero, so rain, drizzle or even humid air can freeze on it. This cold-soak ice is clear and hard to see, and can form on the upper wing with outside temperatures up to about +10 to +15 °C; check it by touch where procedures require. On a clear night, radiation can also cool surfaces several degrees below the air temperature, producing frost. 09.01.01.09

The intensity of icing depends on:

  • the liquid water content: more water, faster accretion;
  • the drop size: larger drops strike more of the surface and further back;
  • the temperature: 0 to −10 °C is worst, colder air holds less water;
  • ice crystals: a cloud that has turned to ice holds less supercooled water, though engines can still ingest the crystals;
  • the aircraft's speed: higher speed sweeps up more water, but kinetic heating raises the surface temperature, by about 1 °C at 100 kt TAS and about 10 °C at 300 kt;
  • the shape of the part: thin objects such as antennas, probes, the tailplane and thin leading edges collect water efficiently and ice faster than a thick wing.

Because the tailplane ices before the wing, extending flap can provoke a tailplane stall. 09.01.01.10

Mountains make icing worse. Air forced up the windward side rises strongly and persistently, condensing more water and holding large drops aloft. The freezing level may be lower over mountains, where cold air pools, and the minimum safe altitude limits any escape downward. The most severe icing is on the windward slopes and just above ridge level. 09.01.01.11

Even stratiform cloud formed over mountains can hold a high concentration of droplets, because the continuous forced ascent keeps supplying vapour to condense. Its liquid water content can approach that of cumuliform cloud, so orographic stratiform cloud can give moderate to severe icing. 09.01.01.12

Exam trap. Stratiform cloud does not always mean light icing. Over mountains it can be moderate to severe.

9.2 Types of ice

Clear ice, or glaze, is a smooth, transparent or translucent, dense, heavy layer, formed when large supercooled drops freeze slowly and spread over the surface before freezing. It is the most dangerous type: heavy, strongly adhering, hard to remove and prone to forming horns. 09.01.02.01

It forms with large drops and high liquid water content, between 0 and about −10 °C (to about −15 °C in Cb), so it is typical of Cu, Cb, Ns and freezing rain. Freezing rain always gives clear ice. 09.01.02.02

When a large drop strikes the surface, only a small part of it freezes at first, about 1/80 of the drop for each degree of supercooling, because the latent heat released warms the rest towards 0 °C. The unfrozen water flows back along the surface and freezes later, with no air trapped in it. That gives dense, clear ice, and runback ice behind the protected areas, beyond the boots or heated zone, where it disrupts the airflow over the wing. 09.01.02.03

Clear ice looks glossy and transparent, smooth or lumpy with horns. It is heavy, with a density close to 0.9 g/cm³, and very hard and firmly stuck. It is hard to see on the wings and is often detected only by ice detectors or on the wipers and probes. 09.01.02.04

Rime ice is white, opaque, rough and granular. It forms when small supercooled droplets freeze instantly on impact, trapping air between the frozen particles, and it builds forward into the airflow on leading edges and probes. 09.01.02.05

Rime forms with small droplets, low liquid water content and temperatures of about −10 to −20 °C or colder, so it is typical of St, Sc, As and freezing fog. In stratiform cloud it can build up over long periods and block pitot and static ports and air intakes. 09.01.02.06

Rime is white, opaque and rough or feathery; light, because it is porous; and brittle, so de-icing systems remove it fairly easily. It is less dangerous than clear ice for weight, but its rough shape still reduces lift and adds drag. 09.01.02.07

Mixed ice is a mixture of clear and rime ice, in layers or patches, often with snow or ice crystals embedded. It forms when drop sizes vary, or when ice crystals and supercooled drops are present together. It is rough and solid, and carries a severe aerodynamic penalty. 09.01.02.08

It forms at about −10 to −15 °C, with varied droplet sizes, in mixed-phase cloud (Cu, Ns, frontal cloud) or where snow mixes with supercooled drops. It is common in frontal Ns and on the flanks of Cb. 09.01.02.09

Mixed ice looks whitish or cloudy, with rough, irregular shapes. It is fairly heavy, hard and firmly stuck, between clear ice and rime, and can build large, irregular horns quickly. 09.01.02.10

Snow at low temperatures is dry and usually does not stick. Wet snow near 0 °C, or snow mixed with supercooled drops, does stick and freeze, building heavy deposits on leading edges, windscreens and engine intakes. On the ground, snow accumulates and can melt and refreeze on cold surfaces. Wet snow can block intakes and pitot heads, and de-icing fluid holdover times are short in snow. 09.01.02.11

Hoar frost is a white, crystalline, feathery deposit of ice formed by deposition: water vapour turning directly to ice on a surface colder than the frost point. There is no liquid stage, so it forms in clear air. 09.01.02.12

On the ground it forms on a clear, calm night when the surface cools by radiation below 0 °C and below the frost point. In flight it forms when a cold-soaked aircraft descends quickly from a cold altitude into warmer, moist air, or climbs from a cold layer into a warmer, moist one through an inversion. The windscreen can frost over suddenly on descent, so use windscreen heat early. 09.01.02.13

Hoar frost is white, feathery and crystalline, thin and light, and only loosely attached, so it is easy to remove; but it must be removed before take-off. Even a thin layer on the upper wing, rough as sandpaper, can cut maximum lift by up to about 30 % and raise the stall speed. 09.01.02.14

9.3 Icing hazards and how to avoid them

ICAO defines three intensities of icing:

  • Light: the rate of build-up may cause a problem if flight continues in it for a long time; occasional use of de-icing or anti-icing removes or prevents it.
  • Moderate: even short encounters become potentially hazardous; de-icing or anti-icing, or a diversion, is necessary.
  • Severe: the de-icing and anti-icing equipment cannot reduce or control the hazard; immediate diversion or exit is necessary.

A SIGMET is issued for severe icing (SEV ICE, and SEV ICE (FZRA) for freezing rain); moderate icing appears in AIRMETs and GAMETs. 09.01.03.01

Ice reduces lift and raises the stall speed (the wing stalls at a lower angle of attack), increases drag and weight, and causes control problems (changed hinge moments on ailerons and elevator, tailplane stall). It ices propellers and engines (power loss, damage from shed ice), blocks pitot, static and angle-of-attack sensors so that instruments become unreliable, obscures the windscreen, damages antennas, and ices the landing gear and brakes. The stall warning may not protect an iced wing, so add the approach speed increments the manual gives, and beware of the autopilot masking control anomalies in severe icing. 09.01.03.02

Clear ice is the most dangerous type: heavy, firmly attached, running back beyond the protected areas and forming horns. Mixed ice has a severe roughness and shape penalty. Rime blocks probes and intakes but is lighter. Hoar frost is dangerous mainly at take-off, through lost lift. Supercooled large drops and freezing rain build ice behind the protected areas and beyond the certification envelope, so leave clear-icing and freezing-rain conditions at once. 09.01.03.03

The dangerous zones are predictable:

  • At a warm front, freezing rain and drizzle fall in the cold air under the frontal inversion ahead of the surface front, and moderate to severe icing lies in the Ns and As near and above the freezing level.
  • At a cold front or occlusion, there is severe clear icing in the Cb and TCU along the front.
  • In cumuliform cloud, the worst icing is in the middle and upper part of the updraft, between 0 and −20 °C, where the water content is highest.
  • In stratiform cloud, it is near the cloud top, where the drops are largest, between 0 and −15 °C. Descending a short distance below the tops often reduces it.
  • In precipitation, freezing rain and drizzle ice the aircraft below the cloud, and wet snow near 0 °C.

The front cross-sections in Chapter 6 show where these zones lie. 09.01.03.04

To avoid icing, start in planning. Study the freezing levels, SIGMETs, AIRMETs and GAMETs, the icing areas on the SWC chart, and pilot reports. Choose a route and level where the air is above 0 °C, below −20 °C, or clear of cloud; consider whether the aircraft is certified for known icing; and avoid areas of freezing rain. In flight, recognise ice early (visual cues, the ice detector, airspeed decay), switch anti-ice on, and change level: climb above the tops or into a warm layer, or into colder air. Change route if necessary, and leave freezing rain at once, by a 180° turn or by climbing into the warm layer if you know where it is. Have an escape plan before you enter icing conditions; aircraft not certified for icing must stay out of known icing. 09.01.03.05

9.4 Ice-crystal icing

At high altitude in and near large convective systems, the air can hold very high concentrations of small ice crystals with little supercooled water. When the crystals enter a turbofan core, some melt on the warm compressor surfaces; the wet surface then catches more crystals, and ice builds up inside the engine. The result can be power loss, rollback, surge, flame-out or damage. Air-data probes such as the pitot and TAT probes can be affected too. The airframe usually shows little or no visible ice, and airframe ice detectors may not trigger. 09.01.04.01

Strong, deep convective updrafts carry large amounts of water to high levels, where it freezes into many small crystals that spread out into anvils and stratiform regions downwind. The ice water content (IWC) is the mass of ice crystals per unit volume of air, in g/m³. Engine events are linked with high IWC, above about 1 g/m³ and up to 3 g/m³ or more. Because small crystals reflect radar energy weakly, high IWC does not show as heavy returns on weather radar. 09.01.04.02

High ice-crystal concentrations are most likely in large tropical convective systems (mesoscale convective systems, the ITCZ, monsoons and tropical cyclones), especially over warm oceans; above and downwind of Cb cores; and in anvils. They are typically met above about FL 200, at temperatures of about −10 to −50 °C, often near or above the freezing level in deep, moist tropical air. Most events happen in tropical and subtropical regions, at cruise altitude. 09.01.04.03

The hazards are engine power loss, rollback or flame-out (often of several engines), engine damage, and air-data errors: a frozen pitot gives unreliable airspeed and disconnects the autopilot and autothrust, and the TAT probe can stick near 0 °C. Other cues are "rain" on the windscreen at sub-zero temperatures, St Elmo's fire, an ozone-like smell, and light to moderate turbulence. 09.01.04.04

To avoid ice crystals, do not fly over or downwind of convective cores, or through anvils. Tilt the weather radar down to look below your level, where the cores are, and increase the gain. Deviate upwind of Cb. Treat areas of weak returns next to strong cells with suspicion, since weak returns in dense, high-altitude cloud near Cb may mean high IWC. Follow the manufacturer's procedures, such as engine anti-ice and continuous ignition. 09.01.04.05

9.5 Turbulence

ICAO defines the intensity of turbulence by its effect on the aircraft and its occupants:

  • Light: slight, erratic changes in altitude or attitude. Occupants may feel a slight strain against their seat belts; loose objects stay at rest.
  • Moderate: changes in altitude or attitude, but the aircraft stays in positive control. Indicated airspeed varies. Occupants feel definite strain against their belts, unsecured objects are dislodged, and walking is difficult.
  • Severe: abrupt, large changes in altitude or attitude and large airspeed variations. The aircraft may be momentarily out of control, and occupants are thrown violently against their belts.
  • Extreme (sometimes added): the aircraft is violently tossed about and practically impossible to control, and may be damaged.

Severe turbulence triggers a SIGMET; moderate turbulence appears in AIRMETs, GAMETs and on the SWC chart. 09.02.01.01

Turbulence rapidly changes the load factor (the gust load grows with gust velocity, true airspeed and the slope of the lift curve), causes airspeed and altitude excursions, and can exceed structural limits, or stall the aircraft when a strong gust meets it at low speed. It can injure crew and passengers, cause loss of control, raise workload and make instruments hard to read. Fly the turbulence penetration speed (VRA or VB), which balances the margin to the stall against the margin to structural limits; hold attitude, not altitude; and disconnect the autothrust if the procedures recommend it. 09.02.01.02

To avoid turbulence, plan with the SWC chart's turbulence, CAT and CB areas, the jet stream positions, SIGMETs, AIRMETs, pilot reports and mountain-wave forecasts. Choose a route and level away from jets, Cb, mountains in strong winds and low inversions with shear. In flight, change level (often by 2000–4000 ft) or track, use the airborne radar for Cb, ask ATC for ride reports, and secure the cabin early. Avoid Cb by at least 10 nm (20 nm for severe storms or at high level), and if overflying, clear the tops by at least 5000 ft if possible. 09.02.01.03

Three words describe related things. Turbulence is random, irregular eddying in three dimensions; it mainly loads the structure and bumps the aircraft. Gustiness is the short-period fluctuation of the surface wind about its mean, which is turbulence near the ground as an anemometer sees it. Wind shear is a change of wind speed or direction over a distance, vertically or horizontally, including updrafts and downdrafts; it changes the aircraft's airspeed and energy, and can produce turbulence. Wind shear threatens performance, by draining energy near the ground, more than it threatens the structure. 09.02.01.04

Turbulence happens on small scales, from hundreds of metres to tens of kilometres, and over short times, below the resolution of forecast models, so turbulence forecasts are not very reliable and are best read as probabilities. Pilot reports (special air-reports and automated reports of eddy dissipation rate) are the main observations, and they let others prepare or avoid it. Always report moderate or severe turbulence with position, level, time and aircraft type. 09.02.01.05

9.6 Clear-air turbulence in flight

CAT (Chapter 2) starts suddenly and without any visual warning. It is usually light to moderate, but occasionally severe, and its vertical accelerations can injure anyone not strapped in. At high altitude its airspeed fluctuations can approach the buffet limits, because the margins between low-speed and Mach buffet are narrow there, and it causes altitude excursions. Keep seat belts fastened whenever seated, and slow to turbulence speed while protecting the buffet margins; descending widens them. 09.02.02.01

To avoid CAT, plan with the SWC chart's CAT areas and jet streams, upper wind charts (strong vertical or horizontal shear, tightly packed isotachs), tropopause breaks, sharply curved upper troughs, mountain-wave areas and pilot reports. In flight, change level by 2000–4000 ft, move away from the jet core (often towards its warm, equatorward side), avoid areas where the temperature changes rapidly, and use reports from ATC and other company aircraft. If climbing or descending makes the temperature change rapidly, you are crossing a frontal or jet zone. 09.02.02.02

9.7 Wind shear

Wind shear is a change of wind speed or direction, or both, over a short distance, including updrafts and downdrafts. Vertical shear is change with height, in knots per 100 or 1000 ft; horizontal shear is change along a horizontal distance, in knots per nautical mile. For an aircraft, what matters is how fast the headwind or tailwind component, and the vertical wind, change along its flight path. Updrafts and downdrafts, as in a microburst, count as wind shear. 09.03.01.01

Low-level wind shear is wind shear along the final approach, along the runway, or along the take-off and initial climb path, typically below about 1600 ft (500 m) above the ground, where the aircraft is low and slow. It is reported in the supplementary part of the METAR (WS R24, or WS ALL RWY), by the ATIS and ATC, and by low-level wind-shear alert systems and Doppler radar. 09.03.01.02

Wind shear forms:

  • in thunderstorms, as downbursts, microbursts and gust fronts reaching 10–20 nm from the cell;
  • along squall lines and active cold fronts, with sharp wind shifts and gusts;
  • across frontal surfaces, most markedly at fast cold fronts, and below the inversion at warm fronts;
  • at low inversions, where calm air at the surface lies under a strong wind above, as with a night radiation inversion and the low-level jet;
  • at sea- and land-breeze fronts;
  • in the friction layer, with strong winds over rough ground;
  • over relief: mountain waves, rotors and lee eddies, and around buildings and hangars near the runway.

The most dangerous is a microburst during approach or take-off. 09.03.02.01

Because of its inertia, an aircraft at first keeps its groundspeed, so a sudden change in the headwind changes its indicated airspeed at once. An increasing headwind or decreasing tailwind raises the IAS and the lift, and the aircraft rises above its path: a performance-increasing shear. A decreasing headwind or increasing tailwind lowers the IAS and the lift, and the aircraft sinks below its path: a performance-decreasing shear, the dangerous one near the ground. A downdraft takes height away directly and changes the angle of attack. A microburst combines all three, in sequence. The classic accident follows that sequence: the crew reduces thrust in the first gain of headwind, and then cannot recover from the tailwind and downdraft that follow. 09.03.03.01

To avoid wind shear, plan with the TAF and METAR (watch for TS, CB, +SHRA, strong gusts and WS reports), SIGMETs, aerodrome wind-shear warnings, pilot reports and alert systems. Delay the departure or approach until a Cb or heavy shower has passed, usually 15–20 minutes; choose another runway or aerodrome; add the gust and wind increments to the approach speed; and use the longest runway. In flight, watch the IAS, groundspeed and vertical speed against what you expect, and heed the predictive and reactive wind-shear warnings. Warning signs on approach are a sudden IAS gain of more than 15 kt, large thrust changes needed to hold the path, groundspeed and IAS diverging, and visible heavy rain shafts, virga or rings of dust. At the first sign, fly the wind-shear escape manoeuvre: TOGA thrust, pitch up towards the pitch limit indicator or stick-shaker, no configuration changes until clear, and do not chase airspeed. 09.03.03.02

9.8 Thunderstorms

Several cloud types warn that thunderstorms are developing: TCU (Cu congestus, growing fast, with hard cauliflower tops); Ac castellanus and Ac floccus, showing instability at mid-levels, often in the morning before afternoon storms; Cb calvus, a developing storm; and Cb capillatus with an anvil, a mature one. Ac castellanus in the morning is a forecasting signal for thunderstorms in the afternoon or evening. 09.04.01.01

Every thunderstorm needs moisture, deep instability and a trigger to lift the air. There are five types:

  • Air-mass (single-cell) storms form when moist, unstable air is heated from below. They are isolated, form on summer afternoons over land (at night over the sea), live 30–60 minutes per cell, and grow in weak wind shear, which is why they die quickly: the downdraft falls back through the updraft and cuts it off.
  • Frontal storms form along cold fronts in lines, or are embedded in warm fronts and occlusions, hidden in Ns and As. They can occur at any time of day and be widespread. Embedded storms are the most insidious, so use the radar.
  • Squall lines are organised lines of multicell storms ahead of a cold front or along a convergence line. They bring severe gusts and hail and last for hours.
  • Supercells are single, very large, long-lived storms with a rotating updraft (a mesocyclone). They need strong vertical wind shear and high instability, and bring large hail, tornadoes and downbursts.
  • Orographic storms form when unstable air is forced up over mountains. They stay nearly stationary over the ridges and peak in the afternoon.

09.04.01.02

9.9 The life of a thunderstorm

A single cell lives about 1–2 hours in all, in three stages:

  1. Cumulus stage (about 10–15 minutes): updrafts only, up to about 3000 ft/min; the cloud grows, but no precipitation reaches the ground yet.
  2. Mature stage (about 15–30 minutes): it begins when precipitation reaches the ground. Updrafts and downdrafts run side by side, with lightning, hail and a gust front, and every hazard is at its worst. The anvil forms.
  3. Dissipating stage (about 30 minutes or more): downdrafts dominate, the precipitation decreases, and the anvil detaches and may persist.

Multicell storms keep renewing themselves for hours, and supercells last hours too. Lightning risk is highest within about 5 °C either side of the freezing level. 09.04.02.01

Exam trap. The mature stage begins when rain reaches the surface. That is the exam's definition.

A supercell develops in four stages:

  1. Initial: a strong updraft grows in an environment with strong vertical wind shear that veers with height, and the updraft tilts the horizontal spin of the sheared air into the vertical.
  2. Supercell: the updraft rotates as a mesocyclone 3–10 km wide. Its updraft and downdraft are separated, so it lives a long time. On radar it shows a hook echo and a bounded weak-echo region (a vault). It produces large hail and an overshooting top, with a wall cloud below its base.
  3. Tornado: the low-level mesocyclone tightens, the rear-flank downdraft wraps around it, and a tornado may descend from the wall cloud.
  4. Dissipating: the downdraft cuts off the inflow, the mesocyclone weakens, and the storm decays or begins a new cycle.

Avoid supercells by at least 20 nm; hook echoes and large hail on the radar mean extreme danger. 09.04.02.02

A fully developed thunderstorm carries every hazard: severe or extreme turbulence, with updrafts and downdrafts of up to 6000 ft/min; severe clear icing between 0 and −20 °C (higher in strong updrafts); hail, including from the anvil and in clear air nearby; lightning, with strikes and temporary blindness; heavy rain, with engine water ingestion and poor visibility; microbursts and gust fronts, giving low-level wind shear; squalls; tornadoes; altimeter errors, from rapid local pressure changes of several hectopascals; static and radio interference; and ice-crystal icing aloft. Never take off or land with a thunderstorm over the aerodrome or approaching within about 5–10 nm. 09.04.02.03

The most dangerous zones of a single cell are its core, at the boundary between updraft and downdraft; beneath the cloud (downbursts and heavy rain); below and downwind of the anvil (falling hail); ahead of the storm along the gust front (wind shear up to 10–20 nm away); and above its top (turbulence and overshooting). In a multicell storm, new cells grow on one flank, usually the right or forward flank in the northern hemisphere (often the south-west or south side); mature cells lie in the middle and dissipating ones on the opposite flank, and the strongest turbulence lies between cells. Do not fly between closely spaced cells or under the anvil, and pass on the upwind side. 09.04.02.04

9.10 Lightning

In fair weather the Earth's surface is negatively charged and the upper atmosphere (the ionosphere) positively, with a field of about 100 V/m at the surface. Inside a Cb, collisions between graupel and ice crystals in the presence of supercooled water separate charge: positive charge collects in the upper part, in the ice crystals of the anvil; the main negative charge sits in the middle, around the −10 to −20 °C level; and a small positive region lies near the base. The ground below becomes positively charged by induction. Most lightning strikes on aircraft happen near the freezing level (within about 5 °C of it), often in or near precipitation. 09.04.03.01

There are five types of lightning: cloud-to-ground (ground strokes); intra-cloud, within one cloud, the most frequent; cloud-to-cloud; cloud-to-air; and upward lightning, which starts from a tall structure or from an aircraft acting as a conductor and travels upward. Aircraft often trigger lightning themselves by bridging regions of different charge. 09.04.03.02

St Elmo's fire is a visible bluish or violet glow, a corona discharge, from the sharp points of an aircraft (windscreen frames, wiper blades, wingtips, static dischargers, the nose) in a strong electric field. It occurs in or near Cb, in snow or ice crystals, and in volcanic ash. It is harmless itself, but it shows that the field is strong enough for a lightning strike, causes radio static (precipitation static), and is a cue of ice-crystal or volcanic-ash conditions. 09.04.03.03

When the electric field exceeds the breakdown strength of air, a stepped leader advances from the cloud in short steps, ionising a channel. An upward streamer from the ground, or from an object, meets it, and a powerful return stroke flows, typically 30 000 A and up to 200 000 A, heating the channel to about 30 000 K. Dart leaders and further strokes may follow. The rapid expansion of the heated channel produces thunder. The time in seconds between flash and thunder, divided by 3, gives the storm's distance in kilometres. 09.04.03.04

A lightning strike usually leaves entry and exit points (burn marks or small holes) on the aircraft's extremities: the nose, wingtips and tail. It can damage the radome, antennas, composite structure and lights; cause electrical and avionics transients and failures; magnetise the structure so that the magnetic compass is in error; and blind the crew briefly. Engine flame-out or fuel ignition is rare, because aircraft are designed against it. At night in a thunderstorm area, turn the cockpit storm lights fully on to reduce flash blindness. After a strike, check the systems and the compass, and have the aircraft inspected. 09.04.03.05

9.11 Downbursts

A downburst is a strong, local downdraft from a convective cloud (a Cb, or even a TCU or cloud producing virga) that spreads out on or near the ground in a burst of damaging, diverging winds. An aircraft flying through it meets a headwind on entry and a tailwind on exit. 09.04.04.01

Downbursts come in two sizes:
