Across a microburst the change from headwind to tailwind can exceed 50–80 kt within a few kilometres. The 4 km (2.2 nm) limit and the 2–5 minute peak are the classic exam numbers. 09.04.04.02

Downbursts come from Cb and heavy showers, and especially from: high-based Cb or TCU above a deep, dry layer, giving dry microbursts with virga, driven by evaporative cooling; heavy precipitation cores, giving wet microbursts, driven by the drag of the precipitation together with melting and evaporation; mature thunderstorms and squall lines; and even TCU with little rain reaching the surface. Virga beneath a high-based convective cloud on a hot, dry day warns of a dry microburst even without a thunderstorm. 09.04.04.03

A downburst develops when falling precipitation drags air down with it, and the rain evaporating (and hail and snow melting and sublimating) into the drier air below the cloud cools that air, making it denser than its surroundings. The heavy air accelerates downward, strikes the ground and spreads out radially, often with a curling vortex ring at its leading edge. The visual cues are a rain shaft curling outward near the ground, a ring of dust, and virga. 09.04.04.04

A microburst is at its strongest for 2–5 minutes and lives about 10–15 minutes in all; a macroburst lasts 5–30 minutes. Waiting about 15–20 minutes after a heavy shower or thunderstorm has passed usually removes the hazard. 09.04.04.05

For an aircraft on approach or take-off, a downburst brings, in turn: (1) an increasing headwind, so the IAS rises and the aircraft climbs above the path; (2) a strong downdraft, so it sinks; and (3) an increasing tailwind, so the IAS and lift fall and the aircraft sinks below the path. The total energy lost can exceed the aircraft's climb capability. On the ground, downbursts bring damaging winds and structural damage. Escape early, with maximum thrust and pitch up to the stick-shaker or pitch limit indicator. 09.04.04.06

9.12 Avoiding thunderstorms

Each type of thunderstorm can be anticipated. Before flight, use the TAF and METAR (TS, CB, TCU, +SHRA), SIGMETs (for obscured, embedded or frequent thunderstorms, or squall lines: OBSC, EMBD, FRQ or SQL TS), the CB areas and tops on the SWC chart, satellite images (overshooting tops, cold infrared tops), radar composites, lightning maps and stability forecasts. In flight, watch Cu growing, anvils and mammatus; use radar information from ATC; and use the airborne weather radar, adjusting tilt, gain and range and watching for attenuation shadows behind strong cells. A lightning detector (stormscope) detects discharges in all directions, including in areas without heavy rain, and complements the radar, though its bearings and ranges are approximate. Remember that weather radar detects precipitation, mainly liquid water: it does not see turbulence, dry hail or ice crystals. Chapter 10 describes both instruments. 09.04.05.01

The techniques for avoiding thunderstorm hazards are:

  • Avoid every Cb by at least 10 nm, and by 20 nm for severe storms, at high altitude or with strong echoes. Deviate on the upwind side where possible.
  • Do not fly under the anvil or overhang, and do not fly between cells less than about 20–30 nm apart.
  • If overflying, clear the top by at least 5000 ft, which is often impossible with tops at FL 400 or above.
  • Do not take off or land with a storm within about 5–10 nm of the aerodrome or approach path.
  • If penetration is unavoidable, fly at turbulence penetration speed and hold attitude, not altitude; set the autothrust and autopilot as the procedures say; switch anti-ice on and cockpit lights fully bright; do not turn back once inside; and take the shortest path through the weakest part (lowest reflectivity), at a level that avoids the 0 to −20 °C band of worst icing and lightning where possible.

09.04.05.02

Exam trap. Never "pass on the downwind side" or "fly below the anvil to avoid the hail". Both are wrong.

9.13 Tornadoes

A tornado is a violently rotating column of air, in contact with the ground, hanging from a cumuliform cloud (usually a supercell Cb). It is often visible as a funnel cloud of condensation, a cloud of debris, or both. Over water it is a waterspout. A funnel cloud that does not reach the ground is not yet a tornado. The METAR code is FC, for funnel cloud (tornado or waterspout). 09.05.01.01

Strong low-level vertical wind shear gives the air a horizontal spin, which the supercell's updraft tilts into the vertical to form the mesocyclone. Stretching the rotating column makes it spin faster (conservation of angular momentum), and its interaction with the rear-flank downdraft concentrates the rotation into a narrow vortex that reaches the ground. The pressure in its core can be tens of hectopascals lower than around it. Tornadoes need a supercell or a strong squall line, not ordinary air-mass storms. 09.05.01.02

A tornado appears as a funnel or rope-shaped cloud hanging from the cloud base, often from a wall cloud, with debris at the ground. It is about 50–500 m across (sometimes more than 1 km). Tornadoes are most common in spring and early summer (April to June in the USA), in the late afternoon and early evening, from mature supercells. They move at about 10–40 kt, in the USA usually from south-west to north-east. Their winds range from about 60 kt to more than 250 kt (EF0 to EF5 on the Enhanced Fujita scale), and their paths are typically a few kilometres long, sometimes more than 100 km. Avoid the parent storm by at least 20 nm. 09.05.01.03

Tornadoes are far more frequent and violent in the central plains of the USA ("Tornado Alley", over 1000 a year), where cold, dry air from the Rockies, warm, moist air from the Gulf of Mexico and strong shear meet. Europe has a few hundred a year, mostly weak (EF0–EF2), though strong ones occasionally occur, and waterspouts are common over the Mediterranean in late summer and autumn. In the exam: tornadoes in Europe are less frequent and usually weaker than in the USA. 09.05.01.04

A dust devil is a small whirlwind, a few metres to tens of metres wide and up to a few hundred metres to about 1000 m tall, formed by intense surface heating in clear air. It is not attached to any cloud, lasts minutes, usually has winds below about 50 kt, and can turn either way. A tornado is attached to a Cb and is far larger, stronger and longer-lived, and mostly turns cyclonically. Dust devils can still upset light aircraft and helicopters near the ground on hot afternoons; the METAR code is PO (dust or sand whirls). 09.05.01.05

9.14 Inversions and performance

A strong inversion on its own affects take-off: climbing out of the cold air into the warmer air above, the density falls, so thrust or power and lift fall and the climb gradient decreases, which is critical for heavy aircraft and obstacle clearance. Haze, fog or smoke beneath it reduce visibility. On approach, entering the cold layer improves performance slightly. An inversion combined with marked wind shear, such as a calm, cold surface layer under a strong wind above (the night low-level jet), adds sudden IAS changes when crossing it, gains or losses depending on the wind direction relative to the flight path, possible sink near the ground, and turbulence at the boundary. The most dangerous cases are climbing out of a calm layer into a tailwind above, which loses IAS at low height, and descending from a strong headwind into calm air, which loses IAS on short final. When the forecast shows strong winds at 1000–2000 ft over a calm surface, expect the shear and brief it. 09.06.01.01

9.15 Flying in the stratosphere

The stratosphere has advantages for jets. It lies above almost all cloud and weather, except overshooting Cb tops; the air is generally smooth, except for CAT near the tropopause and jets and breaking mountain waves; the low density means less drag and better specific range; the constant low temperature (ISA −56.5 °C) helps engine efficiency; there is usually no icing; and visibility is good. Optimum cruise levels for jets lie near or just above the tropopause. 09.07.01.01

Its phenomena influence flight in four ways:

  • Wind: the maximum, at the jet core, is just below the tropopause, and wind decreases with height above it.
  • Temperature: roughly constant or slightly rising with height. Temperatures above ISA reduce engine thrust and the maximum altitude, and raise the speed of sound, changing the relationship between Mach number and TAS.
  • Density: low, so the margin between low-speed and high-speed buffet is narrow (the coffin corner) and the manoeuvre margin reduced.
  • Turbulence: CAT near tropopause breaks and above jet cores, breaking mountain waves, and overshooting tops.

Ozone (which irritates the cabin) and cosmic radiation at high latitudes and altitudes also matter. In turbulence at high level near the buffet limits, descend to widen the margins. 09.07.01.02

9.16 Mountains

Mountains slow and deform fronts. The low-level cold air is blocked on the windward side, so the front may become almost stationary and its passage delayed, while the extra lifting increases cloud and precipitation on the windward slopes (heavy rain or snow). In the lee the front may weaken, through the Föhn effect, and then re-form further downstream, and lee lows such as the Genoa low may develop. The windward side of the Alps or Pyrenees therefore gets prolonged frontal weather, and the lee side improvement, Föhn and turbulence. 09.08.01.01

Mountains bring their own vertical motions, shear and turbulence: upslope and downslope winds (anabatic and katabatic), valley and mountain winds, forced ascent and strong descent across ridges, mountain waves with strong up- and downdrafts, rotors, mechanical turbulence and lee eddies, channelling and Venturi acceleration in valleys and passes, marked shear near ridges and at valley inversions, and convective turbulence over sunny slopes in summer. Cross ridges at a safe height and at 45°, approach a ridge from the upwind side, where the updrafts are, and avoid the lee at low level in strong wind. 09.08.02.01

On a sketch of a mountain chain, the turbulent zones lie as follows. On the windward side there is moderate mechanical turbulence close to the slope. At the crest the flow accelerates, with a cap cloud and strong shear. In the lee a strong downdraft runs down the slope, and rotors lie beneath the wave crests at or below ridge height, with severe or extreme turbulence. Above them is smooth wave flow with lenticulars, and the waves may break at high levels, giving CAT. Sketch questions place the rotor under the first wave crest in the lee; the mountain-wave diagram in Chapter 2 shows it. 09.08.02.02

Relief increases icing. Lifting over mountains produces cloud with high liquid water content and large drops on the windward side and over the ridge; the freezing level may be lower in valleys where cold air pools; and the minimum safe altitude may force you to fly in the icing layer with no escape downward. Plan routes where the minimum safe altitude is below the freezing level, or above the cloud tops. 09.08.02.03

9.17 Valley inversions

At night, air cooled on the slopes drains down into the valley floor and collects as a pool of cold air beneath warmer air on the slopes above (the thermal belt). This makes a strong valley inversion, which traps fog, frost and pollution. Valley aerodromes get radiation fog and low stratus in the morning, while the middle of the slopes may be warmer and clearer. 09.08.03.01

A valley inversion also forms when warm air flows over the valley (warm advection or Föhn) but cannot push out the dense pool of cold air in it. The warm wind blows over the top, making a sharp inversion with strong wind shear at its top and calm, cold air below. In winter such a pool can last for days, and descending from the warm, windy layer into the calm cold pool on approach brings strong shear. 09.08.03.02

For an aircraft, a valley inversion means poor visibility (fog, haze and smoke) beneath it; wind shear and turbulence at its boundary; sudden IAS changes when climbing or descending through it; reduced climb performance on entering the warmer air above; and possible icing in fog or stratus below zero. Brief the shear and the performance change for departures from valley aerodromes in winter. 09.08.03.03

9.18 Visibility

Precipitation reduces visibility by different amounts. Drizzle has many small drops, often with mist or fog, so visibility is often below 3000 m and sometimes below 1000 m. Rain has little effect when light (above 5 km), reduces visibility to 3–10 km when moderate, and when heavy, especially in showers, can bring it below 1000 m and cover the windscreen in water. Snow is the most effective: light snow gives 1–5 km, moderate about 500–1000 m, and heavy snow less than 500 m, down to about 100 m. For the same intensity, snow reduces visibility most, then drizzle, then rain. 09.09.01.01

Obscurations reduce it too:

  • Fog gives visibility below 1000 m, and mist (wet) 1000–5000 m.
  • Haze, of dry particles, typically gives 1–5 km, worse looking into the sun.
  • Smoke (FU), from fires and industry, reduces horizontal and slant visibility, and is often yellowish or brown.
  • Volcanic ash (VA) is made of abrasive glass particles. Besides reducing visibility, it can severely damage engines, abrade the windscreen, block the pitot and cause flame-out. It is often invisible at night or in cloud. Avoid it completely, following VAAC advisories and VA SIGMETs (Chapter 10); its signs include St Elmo's fire, a sulphur smell, dust in the cockpit and rising exhaust gas temperatures.

09.09.01.02

Dust (DU) or sand (SA) suspended in the air, raised earlier by wind somewhere else, makes a dry haze. It can reduce visibility to a few kilometres or less over large areas and for long periods, as with the Harmattan, or Saharan dust reaching Europe. It persists after the wind has dropped; BLDU and BLSA, by contrast, are dust or sand being raised by the local wind at the time of the observation. 09.09.01.03

Meteorological visibility is measured horizontally at the surface. From above a shallow fog or haze layer, a pilot may see the ground straight down, through only a short path in the layer, while the slant visibility along the approach path, a long path through the layer, is much poorer. Inside the layer, flight visibility may differ from the reported ground visibility; above a haze layer, horizontal visibility can be excellent while the ground is hidden at shallow angles. On an approach into shallow fog the runway lights can disappear as you enter the layer, so rely on the RVR and the approach minima, not on what you saw from above. 09.09.01.04

Wind can raise snow, dust or sand. Drifting snow (DRSN) is raised by the wind to less than 2 m; it does not significantly reduce visibility at eye level, but it hides surface features and runway markings. Blowing snow (BLSN) is raised to 2 m or more, and can reduce horizontal visibility below 1000 m even when no snow is falling. It can cause a loss of surface contrast (whiteout) and is reported even under a clear sky. 09.09.02.01

In the same way, drifting dust or sand (DRDU, DRSA) is raised below 2 m, and blowing dust or sand (BLDU, BLSA) is raised to 2 m or more by the local wind, reducing visibility at eye level. On take-off it brings engine ingestion and erosion, and it hides the runway edges. 09.09.02.02

In a dust storm (DS) or sandstorm (SS), strong, turbulent winds raise large amounts of dust or sand to considerable heights, often several thousand feet and up to FL 100 or more. Visibility is generally below 1000 m, and below 200 m when heavy (+DS, +SS). It often arrives with a wall-like leading edge (a haboob, from Cb outflow). Avoid it: aerodromes close, and the dust causes severe abrasion and engine damage. It can arrive suddenly with a gust front. 09.09.02.03

Ice or frost on the windscreen, from supercooled drops, freezing rain, or hoar frost on descent into warm, moist air, can reduce forward visibility to zero, and rain on an unheated screen reduces it too. Switch on windscreen heat before entering icing conditions; hoar frost on descent can form suddenly. 09.09.02.04

Looking towards a low sun, light scattered by haze, dust or a dirty or scratched windscreen dramatically reduces contrast (glare), so visibility into the sun is much worse than down-sun. Landing into a low sun in haze, the runway and other traffic are hard to see; consider the timing and runway direction, and use visors or sunglasses. 09.09.02.05

Sunlight reflected from the tops of haze, fog or cloud layers makes a bright, uniform glare that reduces the contrast of anything below or within the layer and blurs the horizon. Flying just above such a layer, the ground, traffic and terrain are hard to see, and the false horizon risks spatial disorientation. 09.09.02.06

Check yourself

  1. Is carburettor icing likely at +15 °C with a dew point of +13 °C? Yes. That is close to the most likely range: high humidity and temperatures between 0 and +20 °C, especially at low power.
  2. Which type of ice forms in freezing rain, and why is it so dangerous? Clear ice. Large drops freeze slowly and run back beyond the protected areas, forming heavy, firmly attached ice and horns.
  3. In stratiform cloud, where is icing usually worst? Near the top of the cloud, where the drops are largest, between 0 and −15 °C.
  4. Why may high ice-water-content areas look harmless on weather radar? Small ice crystals reflect radar energy weakly, so they show as light returns.
  5. On approach you suddenly gain 20 kt of IAS near a heavy shower. What should you expect next, and what should you not do? A downdraft and then a tailwind, with sinking and loss of IAS. Do not reduce thrust; be ready for the wind-shear escape manoeuvre.
  6. When does the mature stage of a thunderstorm begin? When precipitation reaches the ground.
  7. What is the size limit between a microburst and a macroburst? 4 km (2.2 nm) of outflow.
  8. A storm's flash is followed by thunder 12 seconds later. How far away is it? About 4 km.
  9. Why can the ground be visible straight down from above shallow fog while the approach is impossible? The vertical path through the fog is short, but the slant path along the approach is long, so slant visibility is far worse.

chapters.html:
The last chapter turns from the weather itself to the information about it: how it is observed at the surface, aloft, from satellites and by radar; how it is drawn on charts; the coded messages pilots read every day; and the organisations that produce them. It ends with a decoding self-test. In the exam, many 050 figures are SWC charts, upper wind and temperature charts, surface charts and coded METAR or TAF extracts, so practise reading them.

10.1 Wind and gusts

A gust is a brief increase in wind speed. In a METAR, a gust is reported (G after the mean speed) when the highest 3-second wind in the last 10 minutes exceeds the mean by 10 kt or more, as in 24018G32KT. With a smaller difference, there is no G group. Many operators add half the gust increment to the approach speed, within limits. 10.01.01.01

The METAR wind is a 10-minute mean, with its direction in degrees true, representative of the aerodrome or its main runway. The tower wind, given by ATC or the ATIS for take-off and landing, is a 2-minute mean (with gusts over 10 minutes), with its direction in degrees magnetic, from sensors at the touchdown or departure zone of the runway in use. Where the magnetic variation is large, the two directions differ noticeably. 10.01.01.02

10.2 Visibility

Visibility for aeronautical purposes is the greater of two distances: the greatest distance at which a black object of suitable size near the ground can be seen and recognised against a bright background; and the greatest distance at which lights of about 1000 candelas can be seen and identified against an unlit background. At night, visibility is therefore judged by lights, and can differ from the day value for the same air. 10.01.01.03

It is measured either by an observer, using markers (objects or lights at known distances around the aerodrome), or by instruments (forward-scatter meters or transmissometers) that measure how much the air dims light, the meteorological optical range (MOR), which is converted to visibility. An automatic (AUTO) METAR's visibility comes from sensors that sample only a small volume of air. 10.01.01.04

Prevailing visibility is the visibility reached or exceeded within at least half the horizon circle, or within at least half the aerodrome's surface; those areas need not be adjoining. It is the main visibility in the METAR. If the visibility in one direction is below 1500 m, or below half the prevailing value, the lowest visibility and its direction are also reported, as in 4000 1200SW. Prevailing visibility is not the minimum visibility. 10.01.01.05

Ground visibility is the visibility at an aerodrome reported by an accredited observer or an automatic system. It is what VFR take-off and landing are based on, as opposed to flight visibility, seen from the cockpit in flight. 10.01.01.06

Visibility is reported in metres: in steps of 50 m below 800 m, 100 m up to 5000 m, and 1000 m up to 9999, which means 10 km or more. Plain-language reports use kilometres, and the USA and Canada use statute miles (SM), as in 1/2SM or 10SM. CAVOK replaces visibility, weather and cloud when the visibility is 10 km or more, there is no cloud below 5000 ft (or the highest minimum sector altitude, if higher) and no CB or TCU, and there is no significant weather. 10.01.01.07

10.3 Runway visual range

Runway visual range (RVR) is the range over which the pilot of an aircraft on the runway centre line can see the runway surface markings or the lights that outline the runway or mark its centre line. It is the controlling value for low-visibility approach and take-off minima. 10.01.01.08

Instruments (transmissometers or forward-scatter meters) measure how much the air dims light, and the RVR is calculated by combining that with the intensity setting of the runway lights and the background brightness (day or night). It is reported when the visibility or the RVR is below 1500 m. At night, bright runway lights can make the RVR higher than the meteorological visibility. 10.01.01.09

The sensors stand beside the runway, no more than about 120 m from the centre line, at about 2.5 m height (a pilot's eye height). They are placed at the touchdown zone (TDZ, about 300 m from the threshold), the mid-point (MID) and the stop end (END, about 300 m from the end). The operator's minima say which of these values are controlling, usually the TDZ, with MID and END for some operations. 10.01.01.10

RVR is given in metres in Europe and in feet in the USA. In a METAR, R24/0550U means an RVR of 550 m on runway 24, tending upward; D means downward and N no change. A P before the value means more than the highest value the system can assess (P2000, more than 2000 m; older texts show P1500), and M means less than the lowest (M0050, below 50 m). R24/0550V0800 means the RVR is varying significantly between 550 and 800 m. 10.01.01.11

Pilots receive RVR four ways: in the METAR or SPECI (a 10-minute mean with its tendency); in the local MET REPORT or SPECIAL (1-minute values); on the ATIS; and from ATC by radio, with current values for TDZ, MID and END. On approach, the latest RVR from ATC is the one used for the approach ban. 10.01.01.12

So, compared: ground visibility is the general visibility at the aerodrome; prevailing visibility is the value reached in at least half the horizon or aerodrome; RVR is measured along a particular runway, from a pilot's eye position, at set points, and allows for the runway lights. Where no RVR is available, some approaches may use a converted meteorological visibility (CMV), according to the operator's rules. 10.01.01.13

10.4 Weather and cloud

Present weather is observed by people (precipitation type and intensity, thunderstorms, obscurations) and by automatic sensors: present-weather sensors (forward scatter combined with precipitation detection), precipitation gauges, lightning detectors, ceilometers and visibility sensors. An AUTO METAR may miss some phenomena, such as TCU or small hail; an unknown element is shown as //. 10.01.01.14

Cloud type and amount are judged by an observer or from satellite pictures. The cloud base is measured by a ceilometer (a laser or light pulse, timed on its return), at night by a cloud-base searchlight with an alidade, by ceiling balloons, or from pilot reports. Cloud tops come from pilot reports, satellite infrared temperatures, radiosondes and radar. METAR cloud bases are heights above aerodrome elevation; tops come only from forecasts or pilot reports. 10.01.01.15

Only CB and TCU are named by type in METARs and TAFs (as in SCT025CB), and SIGMETs refer to CB and thunderstorms (as OBSC, EMBD, FRQ or SQL). All other cloud is described only by amount and base. NSC means no significant cloud; NCD, in an AUTO report, means no cloud detected. 10.01.01.16

Cloud amount is measured in oktas, eighths of the sky covered: FEW is 1–2 oktas, SCT 3–4, BKN 5–7 and OVC 8. BKN therefore starts at 5 oktas, more than half the sky. 10.01.01.17

The cloud base is the lowest level at which the obscuration changes perceptibly from clear air or haze to water droplets or ice crystals. It is reported as a height above aerodrome elevation. In fog or heavy snow, it is replaced by the vertical visibility. 10.01.01.18

The ceiling is the height above the ground or water of the base of the lowest layer of cloud below 20 000 ft covering more than half the sky, that is BKN or OVC. A SCT layer never forms a ceiling, and vertical visibility is treated as one. 10.01.01.19

Cloud bases are given in feet, in hundreds in METARs and TAFs (BKN008 is 800 ft), above aerodrome elevation (or above threshold elevation for precision runways where specified, and above sea level for offshore structures). Compare them with decision heights and minimum descent heights, which are above the threshold or aerodrome, not with decision altitudes and minimum descent altitudes, which are above sea level. 10.01.01.20

Vertical visibility (VV) is the greatest distance an observer can see vertically into an obscuring medium such as fog, heavy snow or sand. It is reported when the sky is obscured and no cloud base can be determined: VV002 is 200 ft, and VV/// means the sky is obscured but the value is not available. 10.01.01.21

It is measured by the ceilometer, as the depth its laser penetrates into the obscuration, or estimated by the observer, whenever the sky is obscured by fog or heavy precipitation. VV appears instead of a cloud group, never together with one. 10.01.01.22

It is given in hundreds of feet in METARs and TAFs (VVhhh, so VV001 is 100 ft), and in metres in some local reports. 10.01.01.23

10.5 Temperature and humidity

Air temperature is measured by thermometers (electrical resistance thermometers, thermistors, or mercury and alcohol thermometers) in a ventilated, shaded screen 1.25–2 m above the ground, with maximum and minimum thermometers alongside. Aircraft derive the static air temperature from their TAT probes. METAR temperatures are rounded to whole degrees, with M for minus (M02). 10.01.01.24

Relative humidity is given in per cent and the dew point in °C (°F in the USA). They are measured by hygrometers (capacitive sensors) or psychrometers (wet- and dry-bulb thermometers). The METAR gives temperature and dew point, not relative humidity; estimate RH from the spread (Chapter 3). 10.01.01.25

10.6 Radiosondes

A radiosonde is a small instrument package carried up by a hydrogen or helium balloon, rising at about 5 m/s. It measures pressure, temperature and humidity and radios them to the ground; the wind is found by tracking the balloon (by GPS or radar, a rawinsonde). The balloon bursts at about 25–35 km. Standard launches are made at 00 and 12 UTC worldwide, and their data feed upper-air charts, numerical models and stability diagrams. 10.01.02.01

A sounding is plotted as temperature and dew point against pressure (height). From it you can read the ELR and so the stability, by comparing its slope with the DALR and SALR; inversions and isothermal layers; cloud layers, where temperature and dew point coincide or nearly so (spread 1–2 °C or less); dry layers, where the spread is large; the freezing level, where the temperature curve crosses 0 °C; and the tropopause, where the lapse rate changes to near-isothermal. For icing, look for cloud layers (T close to Td) between 0 and −20 °C. An inversion with moist air beneath it means stratus, fog or haze; with dry air beneath, a clear but hazy sky. 10.01.02.02

10.7 Satellites

Geostationary satellites orbit about 36 000 km above the equator (Meteosat, GOES, Himawari). Each has a fixed view of one hemisphere and sends images every 5–15 minutes, but resolution is poor near the poles, beyond about 60–70°. Loops of their images show how systems move and develop. Polar-orbiting satellites fly at about 800–850 km (NOAA, MetOp). They give high resolution and global coverage, including the poles, but see each area only about twice a day. 10.01.03.01

Satellite pictures are used to locate and track fronts, depressions, jet streams, Cb and convective systems, tropical cyclones, fog and low stratus, volcanic ash and dust, mountain waves (from lee-wave cloud) and icing-prone areas; to estimate cloud-top heights from infrared temperatures; and as input to numerical models and short-range forecasts, especially over oceans and other areas with few observations. Satellites cannot see CAT in clear air. 10.01.03.02

There are three main types of image:

  • Visible (VIS) images show reflected sunlight, so they work only by day. Brightness shows albedo: thick, water-rich cloud and snow are bright, and the texture and shadows of cloud tops are visible.
  • Infrared (IR) images show emitted heat, so they work day and night. Brightness shows coldness: high, cold tops are white, while warm surfaces and low cloud are grey or dark.
  • Water vapour (WV) images show emission from moisture in the middle and upper troposphere (wavelengths of about 6.2–7.3 µm). They show the upper-level flow, dry intrusions and jet streams, but cannot see the surface.

Fog and low stratus are therefore bright on VIS but dark or grey (warm) on IR, so use VIS by day or special fog products at night; a Cb is bright on both. 10.01.03.03

Stratiform cloud looks smooth and uniform, with sharp, straight edges (fog and stratus often follow coasts and terrain), and is uniform grey on IR. Cumuliform cloud looks lumpy, cellular and mottled, with shadows on VIS. A Cb appears bright and rounded, often with an anvil plume and an overshooting top. Polar air over a warm sea shows open cells (rings of Cu around clear centres), while Sc under an inversion shows closed cells; open cellular Cu behind a cold front means cold, unstable air and showers. 10.01.03.04

Fronts appear as long, continuous bands of cloud: a cold front as a narrow band with a sharp rear edge, a warm front as a broad shield of layered cloud ahead of the surface front, and an occlusion as a spiral or comma head around the low centre, with the triple point where they meet. The surface cold front usually lies along the rear, cold-air edge of its cloud band. 10.01.03.05

Atmospheric motion vectors (AMVs) are wind estimates made by tracking cloud or water-vapour features between successive images and assigning them a height. Bands of high-speed vectors at upper levels show the jet axis. In the images themselves, a jet is also marked by sharp boundaries of moisture (on WV) and by cirrus edges and streaks parallel to the flow; it often runs along the poleward edge of a frontal cirrus shield. 10.01.03.06

10.8 Weather radar

A ground weather radar transmits pulses of microwaves (in the S or C band) and measures the energy reflected by precipitation. The reflectivity, in dBZ, relates to the precipitation intensity (it rises with the sixth power of drop diameter), and the delay of the echo gives the range. Doppler radars also measure the speed of particles towards or away from the radar, revealing wind, wind shear and mesocyclones; dual-polarisation radars can tell hail, rain and snow apart. Networks of radars produce composite images. Radar shows precipitation, not cloud: cloud and fog that are not precipitating are invisible to it. 10.01.04.01

On radar images, a colour scale shows reflectivity or rain rate: weak (blue or green), moderate (yellow), heavy (orange or red) and extreme (purple or magenta, which means hail). Convective cells appear as small, intense cores with strong gradients, stratiform rain as wide, uniform areas, squall lines and cold fronts as lines, and bow echoes warn of damaging winds. Animations show movement. Composite images may be several minutes old, so do not use them for close-in avoidance. 10.01.04.02

Airborne weather radar is a nose-mounted X-band pulse radar (about 9.3 GHz, 3 cm wavelength) with a pencil beam about 3–5° wide, scanning ahead through ±60–90°. It shows precipitation intensity in colour levels: green, yellow, red and magenta. Its controls are range, tilt (the beam's elevation) and gain; its modes include WX (weather), WX+T (turbulence, by Doppler) and MAP (ground mapping), and some systems give predictive wind-shear alerts. Use the tilt to scan up and down; at high altitude, tilt down to see the more reflective lower parts of cells. 10.01.04.03

The airborne radar has limits:

  • It detects liquid water best. Dry hail, snow and ice crystals reflect weakly, and CAT and dry turbulence are invisible (except to a Doppler turbulence mode, in rain).
  • Attenuation: heavy rain absorbs the beam, so cells behind it look weaker or vanish (a radar shadow). No return behind a strong echo does not mean no weather.
  • Beam spreading: at long range the beam is wide and can pass over or under cells, and small cells are under-represented.
  • Wrong tilt: the beam can overscan the tops of cells, giving weak echoes at high altitude, or pick up ground clutter.
  • Delay and range: the display lags slightly and the range is limited.

10.01.04.04

On the display, red or magenta means heavy rain or hail: avoid it by at least 20 nm. Shapes that warn of severe turbulence and hail are hooks, fingers (protrusions), scalloped edges, U-shapes or crescents, shapes that change rapidly, and steep reflectivity gradients. Uniform green means stratiform rain. Deviate upwind, well clear of edges with steep gradients. 10.01.04.05

10.9 Air-reports

A routine air-report (AIREP) gives position, time, flight level, wind and temperature (and sometimes more), made at designated reporting points or intervals; today it is mostly sent automatically by datalink (ADS-C, AMDAR). A special air-report (ARS) is made whenever certain hazardous phenomena are met or seen, by voice or datalink, and can trigger a SIGMET. 10.01.05.01

Pilots must make special air-reports when they meet or observe the specified conditions, such as severe turbulence or severe icing, and routine reports where the air navigation services or operations require them. Report as soon as practicable to the ATS unit, with position, time, level and the phenomenon. 10.01.05.02

A special air-report is made for: moderate or severe turbulence; moderate or severe icing; severe mountain wave; thunderstorms, with or without hail, that are obscured, embedded, widespread or in squall lines; a heavy dust storm or sandstorm; a volcanic ash cloud; and pre-eruption volcanic activity or an eruption. (For supersonic flight, moderate turbulence, hail and Cb in the transonic and supersonic phases are added.) The standard abbreviations include SEV TURB, MOD ICE, SEV MTW, TS, TSGR, HVY DS and VA CLD. 10.01.05.03

10.10 Significant weather charts

Significant weather (SWC or SIGWX) charts are forecasts valid at a fixed time. The World Area Forecast Centres issue the high- and medium-level charts, and national MET offices the low-level ones. They show:

  • jet streams of 80 kt or more: an arrow along the axis, wind barbs and flags, the flight level of the core, and sometimes the vertical extent of the 80 kt isotach (as in FL 270/390);
  • tropopause heights, as flight levels in boxes, with H and L centres;
  • CB areas, inside scalloped lines, described as ISOL (isolated), OCNL (occasional, well separated), FRQ (frequent, with little or no separation) or EMBD (embedded in layer cloud), with base and top. XXX means a base or top outside the chart's layer. A CB on the chart implies hail and moderate or severe icing and turbulence;
  • turbulence and CAT areas, inside dashed lines, with intensity and vertical extent, plus icing areas and mountain waves;
  • fronts with their speed and direction, tropical cyclones, volcanoes (with an eruption symbol), sandstorms and sites of radioactive release;
  • on low-level charts, cloud layers (amount, type, base and top), the freezing level (0 °C: FL), visibility and weather.

The high-level chart covers FL 250–630, the medium-level chart FL 100–450 (regional), and the low-level chart the surface to FL 100 (FL 150 in mountainous areas, up to FL 245 for some products). Typical exam figures ask where turbulence is absent at FL 340, what cloud there is at FL 160 over a city, or which is the best level on a route: read the areas, their vertical limits and the jet core's level. 10.02.01.01

To describe the conditions along a route at a given level, draw the route on the chart and check, for your flight level: whether you are inside a CB area, and whether its tops are above your level; whether you are inside a CAT or turbulence area whose vertical range includes your level (MOD 300/400 affects FL 300 to FL 400 only); how close the jet core is and at what level, remembering the shear on its cold side; whether the tropopause is above or below you; and, on low-level charts, the icing areas, freezing level and fronts you will cross, with their speed. Choose a level that avoids CAT areas and stays above or clear of CB tops where possible. 10.02.01.02

10.11 Surface charts

On a surface chart you should recognise ridges (U-shaped isobars extending from a high), cols (between two highs and two lows), troughs (V-shaped isobars extending from a low), and fronts: warm (red semicircles), cold (blue triangles), occluded (purple, alternating), stationary (red semicircles and blue triangles on opposite sides) and upper fronts (open symbols). You should also recognise the frontal side (ahead of the warm front), the warm sector and the rear side (behind the cold front) of a mid-latitude low, and highs and lows with their central pressures. An analysis shows the observed state at a given time; a prognostic (forecast) chart shows the expected state, often with arrows for movement. 10.02.02.01

To find the wind from a surface chart, take the tangent to the isobars with low pressure on the left (northern hemisphere): this is the geostrophic or gradient wind at about 2000 ft. The surface wind is backed by about 30° over land, or 10° over the sea, towards low pressure. The speed comes from the isobar spacing, using the geostrophic wind scale for the chart's latitude (closer isobars, stronger wind), reduced to about 50 % over land or 70 % over the sea at the surface; it is lighter round lows and stronger round highs. Compare spacing only at similar latitudes. 10.02.02.02

10.12 Upper-air charts

A constant-pressure chart shows conditions on a surface of constant pressure, such as 850, 700, 500, 300, 250 or 200 hPa: contours of the height of that surface (isohypses), isotherms, wind barbs and sometimes humidity. The height contours play the part of isobars, and the wind blows along them. The approximate flight levels are 850 hPa ≈ FL 050, 700 ≈ FL 100, 500 ≈ FL 180, 300 ≈ FL 300, 250 ≈ FL 340 and 200 ≈ FL 390. 10.02.03.01

An isohypse, or contour line, joins points where a pressure surface lies at the same geopotential height; on a 500 hPa chart, 552 means 5520 geopotential metres. Low heights mean low pressure aloft and cold air in the column; high heights mean warm air and high pressure. The geostrophic wind on upper charts blows along the contours, with low heights on the left (northern hemisphere). 10.02.03.02

An isotherm joins points of equal temperature on a level or pressure surface. Closely packed isotherms mark a frontal zone, a strong thermal wind, a jet stream above, and a CAT risk; the 0 °C isotherm marks the freezing level. 10.02.03.03

An isotach joins points of equal wind speed. Isotachs show jet cores and wind-speed maxima, and tightly packed isotachs mean strong horizontal shear and CAT. 10.02.03.04

The World Area Forecast System issues forecast upper wind and temperature charts for standard flight levels (such as FL 050, 100, 180, 240, 300, 340, 390 and 450), valid at fixed times (such as 00, 06, 12 and 18 UTC). They show wind arrows or barbs, with direction in degrees true and speed in knots (a half barb is 5 kt, a full barb 10 kt and a pennant 50 kt), and temperatures at grid points in °C. At high levels the temperatures are printed without a minus sign, because they are all negative; a positive value is marked + or PS. 10.02.03.05

To find spot or average values along a route, read the grid values near the route at the right flight level, interpolating linearly between charts for intermediate levels and between points along the route. Average the temperature, and average the wind as a vector (or as its component along the track). Then the ISA deviation is the average temperature minus the ISA temperature for that flight level, never for the true altitude. Average directions and speeds separately only when the directions are similar; otherwise use components. 10.02.03.06

Worked example · route temperature. At FL 300 the temperatures along a route read −40, −44 and −48 °C, a mean of −44 °C. ISA at FL 300 is 15 − 60 = −45 °C, so the route is ISA +1.

10.13 Gridded forecasts

Numerical weather prediction represents the atmosphere on a three-dimensional grid: horizontal points of latitude and longitude, from a few to tens of kilometres apart, and vertical levels of height or pressure. The model solves the equations of motion, heat and moisture at every point, step by step in time. Phenomena smaller than the grid, such as a single Cb or a patch of CAT, cannot be resolved and must be estimated (parameterised). 10.02.04.01

The two World Area Forecast Centres, in London and Washington, produce global gridded forecasts of upper wind, temperature and humidity at standard levels, which flight-planning systems use directly. Flight plans are computed from this WAFS data (in GRIB format), and the SWC charts also come from the WAFCs. 10.02.04.02

The WAFCs also grid the flight level and temperature of the tropopause; the direction, speed and flight level of the maximum wind; the horizontal extent, base and top of CB cloud; icing potential; CAT and in-cloud turbulence potential; and the geopotential altitude of flight levels. These grids are the basis of the hazard layers in electronic flight bags and planning tools. 10.02.04.03

Gridded CB and turbulence data can be displayed as hazard areas on route maps and vertical cross-sections, so crews can see where along the route, and at which levels, hazards are forecast, and choose route and level strategically. 10.02.04.04

Information-processing systems merge these forecast grids with real-time data from aircraft (automated turbulence reports of eddy dissipation rate, AMDAR, pilot reports) and other observations, giving dispatchers and crews (on the EFB) an updated and more accurate picture of the hazards. Real-time reports correct the forecast where it has gone wrong. 10.02.04.05

10.14 Aviation weather messages

The main messages are:

  • METAR: the routine aerodrome observation, every 30 or 60 minutes. Its groups come in this order: type, ICAO identifier, day and time (Z), AUTO if automatic, wind (dddffGfmfmKT, VRB or dddVddd), visibility (with the minimum and its direction), RVR, present weather (intensity or proximity, descriptor, phenomenon), cloud (FEW, SCT, BKN or OVC with height, and CB or TCU, or VV, NSC or NCD), temperature and dew point, QNH (Q in hPa or A in inHg), supplementary information (RE for recent weather, WS for wind shear), runway state, and TREND. CAVOK replaces visibility, RVR, weather and cloud when conditions allow.
  • SPECI: a special observation issued when specified changes occur between routine METARs.
  • TREND: a two-hour forecast added to the METAR, using BECMG (becoming) and TEMPO (temporary fluctuations, each lasting less than an hour and together less than half the period), with FM, TL or AT times. NOSIG means no significant change.
  • TAF: the aerodrome forecast, valid for 9–30 hours (as in 2412/2518). Its change groups are FM (from; a rapid change), BECMG (a gradual change during the period), TEMPO, and PROB30 or PROB40 (probability, alone or with TEMPO). TX and TN give the maximum and minimum temperatures, AMD marks an amended TAF and COR a corrected one.
  • SIGMET: a warning of hazardous en-route phenomena for all aircraft, of three kinds: WS for weather, WV for volcanic ash and WC for tropical cyclones. It is valid for up to 4 hours, or 6 hours for volcanic ash and tropical cyclones.
  • AIRMET: a warning of hazards for low-level flights below FL 100 (FL 150 in mountains) not already covered by the GAMET.
  • GAMET: an area forecast for low-level flights in abbreviated plain language, in two sections: I, hazards, and II, general information.
  • ARS: the special air-report.
  • Volcanic ash advisory: a VAAC message or graphic giving the ash cloud's position and levels now and at +6, +12 and +18 hours.

10.03.01.01

Exam trap. TEMPO in a TAF is not the prevailing condition, and a BECMG change is complete by the end of its period. PROB on its own is only ever 30 or 40 %. In a METAR, 9999 means 10 km or more, and cloud heights are in hundreds of feet above the aerodrome.

Tropical cyclone advisories are issued by the Tropical Cyclone Advisory Centres (such as Miami, Tokyo, New Delhi, La Réunion, Darwin, Honolulu and Nadi). They give the storm's name, its observed position and time, its movement (direction and speed), central pressure and maximum surface wind, forecast positions and winds at +6, +12, +18 and +24 hours, remarks, and the time of the next advisory. The graphical version shows the track and the CB area. The MWO uses the advisory to issue the tropical cyclone SIGMET (WC). 10.03.01.02

The MET REPORT and SPECIAL are the local routine and special reports, in abbreviated plain language, for use at the aerodrome: on the ATIS, by the tower, and for departing and arriving aircraft. They use the 2-minute wind (magnetic for the ATIS) and runway-specific values (RVR by zone, wind by runway end), and are issued when conditions change. The ATIS is built from the MET REPORT, not the METAR. 10.03.01.03

A SIGMET (for subsonic flight) is issued for: thunderstorms that are obscured, embedded, frequent or in a squall line (OBSC, EMBD, FRQ or SQL TS), with or without hail (TSGR); tropical cyclones; severe turbulence; severe icing (including freezing rain); severe mountain wave; heavy dust storms and sandstorms; volcanic ash; and radioactive cloud. An AIRMET (below FL 100, or FL 150 in mountains, for phenomena not already in a GAMET) is issued for: surface wind above 30 kt; widespread surface visibility below 5000 m; isolated or occasional thunderstorms, with or without hail; mountain obscuration; BKN or OVC cloud with a base below 1000 ft above ground; isolated, occasional or frequent CB or TCU; moderate icing; moderate turbulence; and moderate mountain wave. So isolated and occasional thunderstorms go in an AIRMET; frequent, embedded, obscured and squall-line thunderstorms in a SIGMET. 10.03.01.04

The runway state group in a METAR has the form R, runway designator, /, then deposit (1 digit), extent (1 digit), depth (2 digits) and friction or braking action (2 digits):

Key numbers · runway state group (decode with the code table)

Element Codes
Deposit 0 clear and dry · 1 damp · 2 wet · 3 rime or frost · 4 dry snow · 5 wet snow · 6 slush · 7 ice · 8 compacted snow · 9 frozen ruts
Extent 1 = 10 % or less · 2 = 11–25 % · 5 = 26–50 % · 9 = 51–100 %
Depth 00–90 = depth in mm · 92–98 = 10–40 cm · 99 = runway not operational
Friction Two digits = coefficient (45 = 0.45) · 95 good · 94 medium to good · 93 medium · 92 medium to poor · 91 poor · 99 unreliable

Special forms: CLRD (contamination cleared) and SNOCLO (aerodrome closed by snow).

Worked example. R27/290155: runway 27; deposit 2, wet; extent 9, 51–100 %; depth 01, 1 mm; friction 55, a coefficient of 0.55.

10.03.01.05

Since November 2021, Europe reports runway condition with the Global Reporting Format (the runway condition report and SNOWTAM), but the exam still tests the METAR code, with ICAO Doc 7754 as its reference.

10.15 Broadcasts

VOLMET is a continuous VHF broadcast of the current METAR or SPECI and TREND (and sometimes TAF and SIGMET) for a group of aerodromes; it is also available by datalink (D-VOLMET). The ATIS is an automatic, recorded broadcast for one aerodrome, giving its identifier letter, time, runway in use, approach type, surface wind, visibility or RVR, weather, cloud, temperature and dew point, QNH (and QFE), transition level, wind shear, and NOTAM or operational information. It is updated with each new MET REPORT and is also available by datalink (D-ATIS). ATIS winds are magnetic, from the local report; VOLMET relays METARs, so its winds are true. 10.03.02.01

HF VOLMET broadcasts the METAR, TAF and SIGMET for major aerodromes on fixed schedules (at set minutes past each hour) and frequencies, for long-range flights beyond VHF range over oceans and remote areas. It is used to update destination and alternate weather on oceanic crossings, though datalink now often replaces it. 10.03.02.02

10.16 Briefing and in-flight information

Briefing means an oral explanation or consultation with a forecaster, in person or by telephone, or self-briefing through approved systems. Flight documentation is the written, printed or electronic set of charts and messages (METAR, TAF, SIGMET, SWC, wind and temperature charts, advisories) for the planned flight. The commander must study the available meteorological information before flight. 10.03.03.01

Before flight, the MET services provide METARs, SPECIs and TAFs for the departure, destination and alternate aerodromes; en-route SIGMETs, AIRMETs and GAMETs; SWC charts; upper wind and temperature charts; volcanic ash and tropical cyclone advisories; satellite and radar images; and aerodrome warnings. Crews apply them to choose the route and level (winds, CAT, CB, icing), the fuel, the alternates (the TAF must meet the planning minima, including TEMPO and PROB as the operator's rules require), and the take-off and landing performance (wind, temperature, contamination). 10.03.03.02

In flight, crews can receive from the flight information service and ATC: SIGMETs and AIRMETs relevant to the route; special air-reports from other aircraft; aerodrome weather (METAR, SPECI, and TAF on request); ATIS, VOLMET and HF VOLMET; datalink weather (D-ATIS, D-VOLMET, ACARS); and radar weather information from ATC. Use these updates to reassess the destination, alternates and fuel, and decide whether to continue, divert or hold. 10.03.03.03

10.17 Warnings

Aerodrome warnings give concise, plain-language information about conditions that could harm aircraft on the ground (including parked aircraft) and aerodrome facilities: tropical cyclones, thunderstorms, hail, snow (with expected accumulation), freezing rain and drizzle, rime or hoar frost, sandstorms and dust storms, rising sand or dust, strong surface winds and gusts, squalls, frost, volcanic ash and its deposits, toxic chemicals and tsunamis. Wind-shear warnings give observed or expected wind shear, a headwind or tailwind change of more than 15 kt or a significant downdraft, between runway level and about 1600 ft (500 m) along the approach or climb-out path. Wind-shear alerts are automated, up-to-date alerts from ground-based detection systems (LLWAS, Doppler radar, lidar), passed on by ATC, as in "WS ALERT, 30 KT LOSS, 2 MF" (a 30 kt loss 2 nm out on final). Aerodrome warnings concern aircraft on the ground; wind-shear warnings concern the approach and departure paths. 10.03.04.01

10.18 Who provides what

The World Area Forecast Centres, WAFC London and WAFC Washington, run the World Area Forecast System. They prepare global gridded forecasts of upper winds, upper-air temperature and humidity; the direction, speed and flight level of the maximum wind; the flight level and temperature of the tropopause; areas of CB cloud, icing, and clear-air and in-cloud turbulence; and the geopotential altitude of flight levels; and they produce the high-level SIGWX forecasts. These are distributed through SADIS and WIFS. There are only two WAFCs. 10.04.01.01

Aerodrome meteorological offices prepare TAFs, TRENDs, aerodrome warnings and wind-shear warnings, and provide briefing, consultation and flight documentation to crews and operators. The TAF comes from the MET office, not the WAFC. 10.04.01.02

Meteorological watch offices (MWOs) keep a continuous watch over the weather in their flight information regions, issue SIGMETs and AIRMETs (and contribute to GAMETs), and pass them to ATS units and other MWOs. A SIGMET's heading identifies the FIR and the issuing MWO. 10.04.01.03

Aeronautical meteorological stations at aerodromes make the routine and special observations and issue the METAR, SPECI, MET REPORT and SPECIAL. A classic matching question: observations come from the station, forecasts from the MET office, en-route warnings from the MWO. 10.04.01.04

Nine Volcanic Ash Advisory Centres (VAACs), in London, Toulouse, Anchorage, Washington, Montreal, Buenos Aires, Tokyo, Darwin and Wellington, issue volcanic ash advisories, in text and graphic form, with the observed and forecast extent and levels of ash clouds. Europe is covered by VAAC London and VAAC Toulouse. 10.04.01.05

The Tropical Cyclone Advisory Centres (TCACs), in Miami, Honolulu, Tokyo, New Delhi, La Réunion, Darwin and Nadi, issue tropical cyclone advisories with position, movement, intensity and forecasts. MWOs base the tropical cyclone SIGMET (WC) on them. 10.04.01.06

Two international organisations stand above all this. ICAO, the UN specialised agency for civil aviation, sets the standards and recommended practices for aeronautical meteorological services (in Annex 3, Meteorological Service for International Air Navigation, and the PANS), the regional air navigation plans, and the frameworks for the WAFS, the international airways volcano watch and tropical cyclone warnings. The WMO (World Meteorological Organization), the UN specialised agency for meteorology, sets the technical regulations, the codes (the METAR and TAF formats, jointly with ICAO, in its Manual on Codes), the observing networks, data exchange and the training of meteorological staff, and works with ICAO through joint arrangements. 10.04.02.01

10.19 Decoding self-test

Decode each message yourself before reading the answer. The messages are examples written for this text, using the Burgos aerodrome identifier LEBG.

METAR

METAR LEBG 081030Z 24018G32KT 200V280 4000 1200SW R04/0900U -SHRA BKN014 SCT025CB 09/07 Q1008 RERA WS R04 BECMG 6000 NSW

Answer. Routine report for Burgos, 8th of the month, 1030 UTC. Wind from 240° true at 18 kt, gusting 32 kt, direction varying between 200° and 280°. Prevailing visibility 4000 m, with a minimum of 1200 m to the south-west. RVR on runway 04 is 900 m and rising. Light rain showers. Broken cloud at 1400 ft and scattered CB at 2500 ft above the aerodrome, so the ceiling is 1400 ft. Temperature 9 °C, dew point 7 °C. QNH 1008 hPa. Recent rain, and wind shear on runway 04. Trend: becoming 6000 m visibility, with no significant weather.

TAF

TAF LEBG 080500Z 0806/0906 27012KT 9999 SCT030 TX19/0814Z TN06/0906Z TEMPO 0812/0817 4000 TSRA BKN020CB PROB30 0902/0906 0800 FG VV002 BECMG 0818/0820 VRB03KT

Answer. Forecast for Burgos, issued on the 8th at 0500 UTC, valid from 0600 on the 8th to 0600 on the 9th. Wind 270° at 12 kt, visibility 10 km or more, scattered cloud at 3000 ft. Maximum temperature 19 °C at 1400 UTC on the 8th, minimum 6 °C at 0600 on the 9th. Temporarily between 1200 and 1700 UTC: 4000 m in thunderstorms with rain, broken CB at 2000 ft. A 30 % probability between 0200 and 0600 on the 9th of 800 m in fog, with vertical visibility 200 ft. Becoming, between 1800 and 2000 on the 8th, variable at 3 kt. (The TX and TN groups follow the opening conditions, before the change groups.)

SIGMET

LECM SIGMET 3 VALID 081200/081600 LEMD- LECM MADRID FIR SEV TURB FCST N OF N41 FL250/370 MOV E 20KT NC

Answer. SIGMET number 3 for the Madrid FIR, issued by the Madrid MWO, valid 1200 to 1600 UTC on the 8th. Severe turbulence is forecast north of 41° N between FL 250 and FL 370, moving east at 20 kt, with no change in intensity.

GAMET extract

SFC WIND: 30 KT · SFC VIS: N OF N42 3000 BR · SIG CLD: BKN 800/2500 FT AGL · ICE: MOD FL050/080 · FZLVL: 4000 FT AMSL

Answer. Surface wind of 30 kt; surface visibility 3000 m in mist north of 42° N; broken cloud, base 800 ft and top 2500 ft above ground; moderate icing between FL 050 and FL 080; freezing level at 4000 ft above sea level.

Runway state

R22/750193

Answer. Runway 22; deposit 7, ice; extent 5, 26–50 %; depth 01, 1 mm; braking action 93, medium.

Check yourself

  1. The METAR gives 24015KT and the tower 245/15. Why can the directions differ by more than rounding? The METAR is a 10-minute mean in degrees true; the tower wind is a 2-minute mean in degrees magnetic.
  2. Where along the runway is the TDZ RVR measured, and at what height? About 300 m from the threshold, within about 120 m of the centre line, at about 2.5 m height.
  3. FEW005 SCT010 BKN030 OVC080. What is the ceiling? 3000 ft, the lowest BKN or OVC layer.
  4. On a high-level SWC chart, a CB area reads ISOL EMBD CB XXX/400. What does XXX mean? The base is below the chart's lower limit (FL 250).
  5. A TAF has TEMPO 0812/0818 TSRA. For how long, in total, may the thunderstorms last? Each spell less than an hour, and all of them together less than half the 6-hour period.
  6. Is FRQ TS reported in a SIGMET or an AIRMET? A SIGMET. Only isolated or occasional thunderstorms go in an AIRMET.
  7. Why does an area of strong returns sometimes hide another storm? Heavy rain attenuates the radar beam, leaving a radar shadow behind the strong echo.
  8. On a forecast chart at FL 340, a temperature reads 52. What is it? −52 °C: at high levels temperatures are printed without the minus sign.
  9. Which organisation issues SIGMETs, and which produces SWC charts? SIGMETs come from the MWO; high-level SWC charts from the WAFCs.
